titulo: Israel captures top Hamas commander in Gaza strike, defense minister says
texto_limpo:
The Israel Defense Forces captured Hamas' head of general security during a raid in Gaza, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said.
An Israeli security official identified the Hamas leader as Mu'in al-Arabid, head of the General Security Apparatus, saying he was arrested during an Israeli incursion deep inside Hamas territory in Gaza. The IDF carried out airstrikes to cover the raid's withdrawal, adding that there were no Israeli casualties.
"A short time ago, a senior Hamas terrorist was arrested, and this is our policy: We do not wait for threats. Instead, we pursue Hamas terrorists, thwart them, and destroy their terrorist infrastructure. We have built a strong and unprecedented security zone in Gaza to protect residents and IDF soldiers," Katz said in a statement.
HAMAS STRUGGLES TO FILL LEADERSHIP RANKS AS ISRAEL HUNTS OCT 7 TERRORISTS
"Nearly 70% of the Gaza Strip has been destroyed, with no residents, no tunnels, and no homes, and the IDF controls the territory. We are not leaving Gaza until the Strip is demilitarized, Hamas is disarmed, and all terrorist tunnels are destroyed. Even after that, the IDF will remain in Gaza along defensive lines and ensure the security of the western Negev communities. Any attempt to bypass the security zone through aerial launches will be met with a harsh response," he added.
The raid comes weeks after President Donald Trump's administration demanded that Hamas disarm and give up control of Gaza in August. Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, traveled to Israel last month and said the IDF may receive U.S. backing to "finish the job."
NETANYAHU REJECTS BOARD OF PEACE'S GAZA PLAN: NO 'WITHDRAWAL UNTIL HAMAS IS GENUINELY DISARMED'
"If they don't follow through now on their commitment, everyone will see that they're not genuine about peace, and then Israel will have a lot more support from the U.S. and others to go and finish the job in the appropriate way," Kushner also told Fox News' Trey Yingst of the terrorist group.
The warning from Trump's son-in-law followed a rare face-to-face meeting with Hamas in Egypt - only Kushner's second known meeting with the group.
KUSHNER TOUTS UNPRECEDENTED IRAN CONTACTS AS TEHRAN DENIES TRUMP BACKCHANNEL
"They said all the right things, but obviously, it's very, very hard to trust, you know, a terrorist organization that committed these terrible atrocities," Kushner continued. "But we had a very cordial meeting, and they said all the right things, and so we're going to give them a chance to perform."
"It's going to have to be based on actions and steps, and I hope it will be true."
The U.S.-led "Board of Peace" proposal centers on a phased ceasefire, demilitarization of Gaza, Israeli troop withdrawal, Palestinian technocratic governance and international reconstruction efforts.

titulo: Michael Rapaport slams 'clown' Macklemore for anti-Israel performance
texto_limpo:
Michael Rapaport slammed Macklemore as a "clown" after the rapper brought his pro-Palestinian message to Ed Sheeran's concert stage.
Macklemore, 43, repeatedly called to "Free Palestine" and performed his anti-Israel song "Hind's Hall" while opening for Sheeran, 35, at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, during shows on Friday and Saturday nights.
On Saturday, Rapaport, 56, who is Jewish and has become one of Hollywood's most outspoken pro-Israel voices since Hamas' October 7 attack, ripped Macklemore, born Benjamin Haggerty, in a blistering post on X.
BLACK CROWES FACE BACKLASH AFTER CHRIS ROBINSON SHUTS DOWN U.S.A. CHANT AND CALLS FANS 'IGNORANT'
"Imagine going to see Ed Sheeran & this absolute no talent none singer non rapping non dancing clown Macklemore is opening & because he actually has no act or specific skill set he's jumping around like dkc carrying on about a genocide that never happened in Gaza," Rapaport wrote, adding "This is a nightmare."
In another critical post on X, the comedian questioned Sheeran's decision to bring Macklemore on as an opening act.
ED SHEERAN CONCERT WORKERS HOSPITALIZED AFTER FORKLIFT INCIDENT IN DETROIT: REPORT
"So Ed Sheeran is ok with this p--- stain opening up for him? Sweet Ed Sheeran?" Rapaport wrote.
Rapaport also reposted an article about the backlash to Macklemore's political messaging following the concerts, writing, "Calling this dude a 'Rapper' is disrespectful to any actual 'Rapper.'"
ISRAEL, JEWS TARGETED WORLDWIDE AS WELL-FUNDED LEFTIST, ISLAMIST GROUPS JOIN FOR 'NAKBA 78' PROTESTS
Fox News Digital has reached out to Macklemore and Sheeran's representatives for comment.
In a video that Rapaport posted from the Friday night show, Macklemore, who wore a keffiyeh tied around his neck, was seen repeatedly chanting "Say free, free Palestine!" while music played as he walked around the stage and held up his microphone.
Macklemore, who will be opening for Sheeran during the U.S. leg of the "Shape of You" singer's "Loop Tour," also delivered a speech in which he said that he wanted to use stages across America to advocate for Palestine.
ISRAELI PM NETANYAHU ARGUES PUBLIC OPINION SHIFT ON ISRAEL 'CORRELATES ALMOST 100%' TO SOCIAL MEDIA
"A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: Free Palestine," Macklemore said in a video shared on social media.
"I said, 'Free Palestine!' I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them," he continued.
"I have an 11-year-old daughter, her name is Sloan, she's here tonight. And if any of you guys are parents, then you know that that love that you have for your kids cannot be put into words, right? I want to see her grow up, I want to see her go to school, to fall in love, to figure out meaning, purpose, joy, her existence on this planet. I want it to be the most beautiful possible."
"And I think that every single human being that walks this earth deserves that exact same feeling. To know safety and peace before they know the sound of violence, to know the sound of laughter on a playground before planes and bombs, for parents to be able to say bye to their kids in the morning and not have to wonder if this is going to be the last time they kiss their child goodbye."
"And if I let that fear I felt on the plane yesterday stop me from speaking my heart in order to keep my own comfort and the audience's comfort, that is the day I no longer continue to be on stage," Macklemore added. "So, I say, 'Free Palestine!'"
RAGE AGAINST THE MACHINE'S TOM MORELLO FACES BACKLASH AFTER SINGING AT NYC ICE PROTEST RALLY
Macklemore concluded his speech by calling for the freedom of other countries, including America, and blasting U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
"I say, free America, free Cuba to the Congo to Sudan to Iran, and all the people in America who have to live in fear because of this terrorist organization, ICE," he said.
Following his speech, Macklemore performed "Hind's Hall," a song inspired by the 2024 pro-Palestinian campus demonstrations," as footage from Gaza, pro-Palestinian protests, images of Israeli soldiers and pro-Palestinian messages were displayed on the stadium's large screens.
The title of the song refers to Hamilton Hall, the Columbia University building that pro-Palestinian students occupied in <DATE> and renamed in honor of a 6-year-old Palestinian girl killed in the Israel-Gaza war. The lyrics in "Hind's Hall" praised the anti-Israel encampments and protests on college campuses across the country and called out President Biden, the police and the music industry.
RAPPER FACES $2.8M LAWSUIT AFTER AXING OPENING ACT FROM TOUR FOLLOWING HER POLITICAL RANT
Macklemore also repeated his pro-Palestinian messaging during Sheeran's second MetLife Stadium show Saturday night, again calling for "Free Palestine" and performing his protest song "Hind's Hall."
While some audience members cheered Macklemore's comments and joined the "Free Palestine" chant, the rapper's performance was met with backlash from other attendees.
One concertgoer said on X that he brought his wife and two daughters to Friday's show as longtime Sheeran fans, but left disappointed after Macklemore's set turned political. The fan said his daughters looked "completely confused" when Macklemore began chanting "Free Palestine," adding that he had taken them to "an Ed Sheeran concert, not to have an opening act lecture them about Middle East politics."
He said his family left their seats during Macklemore's performance and returned after the rapper finished, praising Sheeran's show as "phenomenal" but criticizing the singer for allowing Macklemore to perform again Saturday. "Friday might have been Macklemore's decision. Saturday was yours," the concertgoer wrote, adding, "Tonight, you lost four of them. And I suspect plenty more."
Another concertgoer said he attended Saturday's show in a company suite with 35 other people and was "embarrassed" and "shocked" by Macklemore's set. The attendee said he had "always been a Macklemore fan," but after the rapper's "political stunt," he could no longer support him or his music.
"When you go WOKE, you have to be prepared to lose fans," he wrote.
The concertgoer also denounced Sheeran for allowing Macklemore to return to the stage Saturday after the backlash from the previous night.
"After it happened on Friday, it should have immediately been stopped," he wrote, adding that he went to the show to hear "amazing music," not "Free Palestine" rants.
Two other concertgoers told Ynet, the English edition of Israel's largest new website, that they were unfamiliar with Macklemore before the show and unaware that he would be performing.
"We only found out there and we were in shock. It was really horrifying," they said.
"We immediately thought about everything our people have been through and how, even when we're abroad, we still have to feel this antisemitism," they continued. "It was even harder because friends of ours were killed in the war and murdered at Nova. It was like a knife in the heart to hear him sing that way and hear people cheering."
The concertgoers said that some of the members in their group began crying and left the show before Sheeran's performance.
However, some social media users praised Macklemore for speaking up and expressed their support for the rapper's message.
"Huge respect for Ed Sheeran, but seeing Macklemore use his voice for Palestine made this moment mean so much more," one fan wrote on Instagram. "Respect to every artist who refuses to stay silent and uses their platform to speak up for humanity. Macklemore, we hear you."
"LOVE Macklemore, and good on him using his platform to speak out....his messaging is always spot on. Peace," another agreed.
"Free free Palestine. Love to Macklemore. Stay true," one fan chimed in.
"this was from last night!! I hope you get to perform this again tonight too!" a fan wrote alongside a clip from Macklemore's set.
"So happy we get to witness such history!" one fan commented.
"Honestly I loved this part of the concert !" another wrote.
"Music has always been a vital platform for human rights advocacy, not just mindless escape," wrote one X user. "Calling for peace, safety, and equality for Palestinians, Congolese, and Sudanese isn't antisemitic - it's pro-humanity. Macklemore explicitly stands for collective liberation and love."
"Art has always been political, why are you annoyed at an artist giving context to a song he released about the current state of the world you live in?" another fan commented on X. "Also, he was an opener, they could've just skipped his set! Although I hope Macklemore sings it louder next time!"

Meanwhile, the Israeli-American Council launched a petition calling for Macklemore to be removed from Sheeran's remaining tour dates.
"This was an Ed Sheeran concert - not a political rally, not a protest, and not an activist event," the petition read. "The issue is not whether Macklemore has the right to hold political views. The question is where the line should be drawn when an opening act uses a global concert platform to advance a one-sided political agenda."
Macklemore has been outspoken in his support for Palestinians since the start of the Israel-Hamas war. In <DATE>, Macklemore spoke at a pro-Palestinian rally in Washington, D.C., where he said, "I don't know enough. But I know enough that this is a genocide."

The rapper's political messaging has also sparked backlash before. In 2024, he addressed criticism after saying "f--- America" during a pro-Palestinian charity concert in Seattle, later writing that he remained "unwavering in my support for a Free Palestine."

Israel has been accused by some human rights groups, legal scholars and foreign governments of committing genocide during the war in Gaza due to the scale of Palestinian deaths, widespread destruction and mass displacement.
South Africa brought a genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice, which ordered Israel in 2024 to take steps to prevent acts of genocide while the case proceeds. Israel has strongly denied accusations of genocide, saying its military campaign is directed at Hamas, not Palestinian civilians, and that it warns civilians to evacuate ahead of attacks while taking steps to comply with international law.

titulo: Pink hits back amid backlash for criticizing Macklemore's pro-Palestinian concert remarks
texto_limpo:
Pink is doubling down on her criticism of Macklemore following his pro-Palestinian comments during a recent concert.
On <DATE>, Macklemore opened for Ed Sheeran at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, and he used his time onstage to perform his anti-Israel song, "Hind's Hall." He repeatedly chanted "Free Palestine" while a slideshow played on the screen behind him, showing footage from the war in Gaza.
Several fans were upset by the performance, including an Instagram page called "Stop Antisemitism." The page shared a video criticizing Macklemore, calling the move "awful." Pink reposted the video to her own Instagram story, which started a new wave of backlash from people criticizing her for seemingly being pro-Israel.
MICHAEL RAPAPORT SLAMS 'CLOWN' MACKLEMORE FOR ANTI-ISRAEL PERFORMANCE
Initially, Pink didn't explicitly share her opinion on the matter, but on <DATE>, she took to Instagram to explain her thoughts in an emotional statement.
"I've been quiet in my own words for a week, which you know isn't like me. So here they are," she began.
The "So What" singer explained that she'd reposted the video that was critical of Macklemore, which "said things in words I didn't write, and I wouldn't have chosen all of them."
She maintained that "a repost isn't a statement," then wrote, "I'd rather be disagreed with for what I actually said than hated for what anybody else wrote, so let me say it."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
"I was born a Jew," she continued. "I didn't pick it, and I've never hidden it. And this week a whole lot of people decided what I believe without asking me, without checking a single thing I've ever said or done, because a repost and the word 'Jew' were apparently enough to fill in the rest. But let me fill it in... myself."
"Of course I don't speak for Israel, or for any government. I never have. What I said in <DATE> is still exactly what I believe: Hamas is a terrorist organization. Palestinians deserve a future that honors their humanity and their aspirations. Protecting innocent life comes first, everywhere, and nobody should ever celebrate the death of a child. Anybody's child."
JERRY SEINFELD GIVES BLUNT THREE-WORD RESPONSE TO INFLUENCER ASKING FOR A 'FREE PALESTINE'
She detailed the work she's done with UNICEF over the years, spending time with children "on both sides of that fence," and said, "I'm not going to litigate a complex war in an Instagram caption, and I'm not going to recite anybody's slogan to earn back a follower."
Pink went on to explain that what she was "reacting to" was Macklemore himself. She recalled him performing his song "Same Love" at the Grammys in 2014, and how she cheered on the message, but "Four months later Macklemore put on a hooked nose, a black beard and a bowl cut, performed in it, and called it a 'random costume.'"
"Every Jew I know knew exactly what it was. The same love, it turned out, had a guest list, and we weren't on it. But he apologized, and I let it go, because that's what we do. We let it go. Then last weekend he stood in front of a stadium full of music-loving families, with violent images from a war on the screens, dedicated a song to the movement of his choice, and then took the mic to tell all of the Jews in the stadium that it wasn't about them."
She added, "You don't get to decide that for us."
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
"That's what prompted my repost," she wrote. "Not 'Free Palestine,' and not anyone's right to say it. I have never asked for another artist to be silenced and I'm not asking now. I don't need anyone fired, and I don't need a refund. What I need is to be able to say, as a Jewish mom, 'that scared me, and it scared people I love,' without being told our fear is just propaganda, and without being told I'm somehow cool with genocide because I noticed?"
Pink wrote that she's always stood up for her beliefs, even when she is criticized for it, citing her own protest song, "Dear Mr. President," which she wrote in 2006 in response to the Iraq War.
"I have stood up for other people's people my whole career, and I know exactly what it costs," she said. "And now I'm standing up for my own people, and I thought I knew going in how lonely that would be. And it's lonelier than that. But I'm doing it anyway."
"Something has changed in this country, and I can read it in my own comments. 'From the river to the sea.' 'Zionist,' spat like it's a slur, by people who couldn't tell you the details of what I believe, because I hadn't told them yet. I wasn't asked. I was told. I don't think most of them hate Jews. I think somebody handed them a story where the Jew who won't apologize for existing must be the villain, and they've been putting words in my mouth ever since."
She said that while she can take being portrayed as a villain, "I just won't take it quietly, and I'm not going to teach my kids to."

Pink added, "So, to the ones who are furious with me: you don't have to agree with me. You never did. That's been our unspoken agreement for twenty-five years, and it still stands, and so do I. You don't have to agree with one thing Israel's government does to not want the Jewish family two rows down from you to be scared or targeted at a concert. That's the only thing I'm asking anybody for. To the ones who are frightened this week, Jewish or Muslim or Palestinian or Israeli or just tired of all of it: I see you. And if anybody wants to really know what I think, just ask me. I'm right here. I've never been hard to find. And I'll keep speaking out, in my own words."
She ended her post by acknowledging the anniversary of 9/11, as well as Rosh Hashanah, saying, "Now I'm going to go make dinner for my kids, light the candles, dip some apples in honey, pour a glass of wine and be full of gratitude. That's my tradition. It also happens to be a Jewish one. Shana tova."
Following the original wave of backlash against his performance, Macklemore shared a video to Instagram of himself speaking onstage, explaining that one of the reasons he chose to tour with Sheeran was to be able to say "Free Palestine" in front of a large audience.
"Wanting all humans to be treated equal should never be controversial," he wrote in his caption.

titulo: 'Nobody Wants This' star accuses Israel of 'genocide'
texto_limpo:
On Friday, Jewish actor Adam Brody joined the growing list of progressive celebrities accusing Israel of committing "genocide" in Gaza while suggesting that Hollywood has grown more "conservative" under President Donald Trump.
Brody, who plays a rabbi in Netflix's romantic comedy series "Nobody Wants This," addressed the topic when speaking to GQ Magazine about his political activism and volunteer work for the progressive organization Swing Left. Although he has not publicly addressed the Middle East conflict previously, Brody told the magazine that he has discussed it privately.
"Put me down as thinking it's a genocide," Brody said. "Put me down as wanting a free Palestine. It's awful that it's taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it's reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago. I'm hopeful that another administration can really do some good and correct some of these policies that are helping that situation be as awful as it is."
"The O.C." actor's comments resembled ones made by other progressive celebrities such as actor Mark Ruffalo and rapper Macklemore, who have referred to the Israel-Hamas conflict as a "genocide."
Though several celebrities have spoken out against Israel's actions, Brody suggested that political activism in Hollywood has decreased, noting that he doesn't speak about political issues in many interviews.
"I think it's the cycle. The first time Trump was elected, it was inconceivable. It woke everyone," he said. "There was so much activism. People were running for office that had never ran before. It was so awful to watch him defile our government, our country, our reputation, and really pit people against each other. I felt like most of the country right away was really against it."
"It felt very safe to step out against him in the first presidency," Brody continued. "The second time, the presidency was more powerful. Corporations were lining up behind him like they hadn't before. People had to risk more to get in front of it. It just felt like the mood wasn't there. The country decided this is the way it wants to go. As we start to pick up steam for this election, it's getting exciting again. We're starting to feel powerful again."
'SHE-HULK' STAR SLAMS TOM SELLECK, MICHAEL JORDAN AS 'COWARDLY' FOR AVOIDING POLITICAL TALK
Brody even claimed that Hollywood has gotten more "outspokenly" conservative during Trump's second term.
"Again, as one side has more power, it makes sense that it draws people to it for all the human reasons that would be attractive: groupthink, your own well-being, your own money and success," Brody said.
Fox News Digital reached out to Brody's representatives for comment but did not immediately receive a response.
In response to the interview, "Hollywood in Toto" founder Christian Toto told Fox News Digital that while it has gotten "microscopically better" to be a conservative in Hollywood, groupthink and bullying behind the scenes "remain powerful" as activism starts to see a resurgence.
MICHAEL RAPAPORT TELLS CRAIG CARTON THAT HIS SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL HAS COST HIM WORK IN HOLLYWOOD
"Hollywood activism was a bit muted following the 2024 election, but now it's back to its usual volume and cadence. And if Brody truly felt afraid to say what he's saying ... he would keep it all to himself. Sharing his doctrinaire, hard-Left views is the most pro-career move an actor can make in 2026, particularly in how he's viewed by fellow actors," Toto said.

titulo: Abdul El-Sayed hits back at Israel questions, suggests his name and faith are behind press scrutiny
texto_limpo:
Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed suggested that reporters press him about the Israel-Hamas war because of his name and his faith.
Speaking on Detroit Public Radio's "MichMash" podcast, El-Sayed pushed back on host Zach Gorchow's line of questioning about the Israel-Hamas conflict, suggesting that his name and Muslim faith play a role in the media attention surrounding the issue.
"You've been asked many times whether you support a two-state solution regarding the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, and you generally say you support equal rights to self-determination for Jewish Israelis and Palestinians," Gorchow said. "Can you tell us, what does that mean?"
"Zach, with all due respect, this has been hashed and rehashed," El-Sayed began. "This is the 'MichMash' podcast. I'm focused on what's happening for the 10 million people in this state."
El-Sayed then suggested the media's interest in his stance on the conflict was related to his identity.
MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE CONFRONTED REPEATEDLY OVER ISRAEL'S RIGHT TO EXIST, DEFUNDING THE POLICE
"It's so frustrating to me that people want to make this race about something that's happening 6,000 miles away, when we've got kids who can't afford a next meal here at home," he continued.
The controversial candidate went on to blast the constant line of questioning from members of the press regarding his stance on providing aid to Israel, a topic he has remained staunchly against throughout his campaign.
MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL CALLS AIPAC DONATIONS 'LEGALIZED BRIBERY,' REMAINS SILENT ON OTHER DONATIONS
"I just find it so interesting that I never get asked about this question on the stump," El-Sayed told the host. "But it seems to me that every time I sit down with anybody in the press, it seems that that's the most important question."
El-Sayed continued by suggesting the media's focus on his stance on Israel could be related to his name and Muslim faith.
EL-SAYED'S HASAN PIKER PROBLEM FOLLOWS HIM TO DEM CONVENTION AS JEWISH VOTERS BREAK RANKS
"It tends to be the first question everybody likes to ask me," he said. "I wonder why. I mean, does it have something to do with my name? Maybe, you know, how I pray?"
He concluded by doubling down on his assertion that his campaign is focused on the people of Michigan, not the people of Israel.
MICHIGAN DEMOCRATIC SENATE CANDIDATE CLAIMS ISRAEL 'JUST AS EVIL' AS HAMAS
"It's fascinating to me that I'm running to represent 10 million people who live here, and you want to ask about people living somewhere else," El-Sayed continued. "And I just think I want to be talking about [the] people living here."
According to data compiled by the Jewish Virtual Library, Michigan is home to 129,225 Jewish residents who comprise roughly 1.3% of the state's population.
JEWISH DEMOCRATS ABANDON EL-SAYED FOR GOP RIVAL IN ALL-IMPORTANT BATTLEGROUND STATE
El-Sayed's comments were of interest to CEO of Axia Public Relations Jason Mudd, who told Fox News Digital his ability to flip the narrative on the press shows a level of message discipline.
"He stayed on message, pivoting to affordability both times he was asked. That's real discipline. But when you listen to the full episode, he never uses the word racist. He questions why the topic keeps coming up and ties it to his name and his faith. He's pointing to bias.
"If El-Sayed were my client, I'd advise him to name the bias claim directly instead of leaving it implied, then answer the follow-up on what his position actually means in the same breath. Right now, the framing comes first, and he still hasn't answered the follow-up."
Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed's campaign for comment.

titulo: Raskin calls Piker’s rhetoric 'irrelevant distraction' after the streamer said he'd vote for Hamas over Israel
texto_limpo:
Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., dismissed scrutiny of far-left streamer Hasan Piker's rhetoric about Hamas as an "irrelevant distraction" Sunday on NBC's "Meet the Press," as host Kristen Welker pressed him over Democratic divisions surrounding Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed's relationship with the controversial online personality.
Welker played Raskin a clip of Piker saying he would vote Hamas over Israel "every single time" and asked whether the Democratic Party's tent was large enough to include the streamer.
"I don't even know if Hasan Piker considers himself a Democrat. I know he attacked me for campaigning with Callie Barr and Sean McCann and other Democrats in Michigan. I think all of that is an irrelevant distraction," Raskin said. "Obviously, nobody supports Hamas, a terrorist organization which brutally attacked Israel on October 7."
Natalie Baldassarre, national press secretary for the RNC, pointed to Piker's growing role in Democratic politics and his support for socialist candidates as she warned that his influence could become a broader liability for the party heading into November.
"The Democrat Party is being driven off [a] cliff by socialists who are driving blindfolded while arguing about the view," Baldassarre said in a recent statement to Fox News Digital. "Unless Democrats hit the brakes, every candidate on the ballot will have to answer for socialists' outrageous beliefs that will bankrupt our country and strip every American of safety, sanity, and freedom."
Raskin's comments came after he campaigned alongside El-Sayed in Michigan in late August. El-Sayed has continued to face questions over his ties to Piker as some Democrats have publicly distanced themselves from the streamer.
Piker, who endorsed El-Sayed and appeared at multiple campaign events during the Democratic primary, reiterated his comparison between Hamas and Israel during an April appearance on "Pod Save America."
"I've also said I'm a harm reduction voter. I'm a lesser evil voter, and therefore I would vote for Hamas over Israel every single time," Piker said in the clip played for Raskin on Sunday.
Piker has also faced renewed criticism for comments involving American Jews. Fox News Digital reported that he warned on a livestream that if American Jews continued presenting themselves as "singularly invested in Israel," someone could eventually "take action" against them.
HASAN PIKER INSISTS ABDUL EL-SAYED ASKED HIM TO 'STUMP' FOR MICHIGAN CAMPAIGN AMID BACKLASH
El-Sayed responded to that controversy by stressing that the streamer was not a spokesman for his campaign.
"I want to be crystal clear, nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople," El-Sayed said.
El-Sayed has nevertheless resisted calls to fully disavow Piker. During a recent interview with Stephen A. Smith, he said his goal was to bring the streamer's millions of listeners into the electoral process rather than abandon them over disagreements.
"What I'm saying is there are 3 million people who listen to Hasan," El-Sayed said. "I want to offer them a pathway into an electoral movement."
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., called the attention devoted to Piker "absolutely ludicrous," while Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash, said Democrats should engage his audience even if they disagree with some of his views. Other Democrats have urged the party to distance itself from him.
Fox News Digital reached out to Piker for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

titulo: Ms Rachel says backlash over her Gaza posts 'doesn't faze' her as she calls out celebrity silence
texto_limpo:
Children's YouTuber star Ms. Rachel told Rolling Stone magazine on Tuesday that the backlash she received for her social media posts on Gaza "doesn't faze" her too much anymore.
The magazine reported that although Ms. Rachel, whose real name is Rachel Griffin Accurso, has spoken out on other political issues such as the Trump administration's deportation policies or LGBTQ activism, her comments on the Israel-Hamas war drew the most "aggressive criticism."
She remarked that the backlash surprised her initially.
"I thought everyone hated me at one point," Accurso said. "I remember calling friends and family members, Jewish and not Jewish, and just being like, 'Why do people hate that I don't want kids to be killed and starved?'"
YOUTUBE STAR MS RACHEL DECLARES 'I AM POLITICAL' IN NEW MISSION TO SHUT DOWN ICE FACILITY
Accurso continued advocating for Palestinian children in Gaza, calling out celebrities and politicians for not speaking out enough on their behalf.
"'You're gonna lose this partnership. You're gonna lose views.' That doesn't faze me because the kids gave me the platform. I'm going to stand with them no matter what," Accurso said. "People on the ground in Gaza are risking their lives all the time to help kids. I can do it from Manhattan."
Fox News Digital reached out to Accurso for comment but did not immediately receive a response.
CHILDREN'S YOUTUBE STAR 'MS. RACHEL' TALKS TO ANTI-ISRAEL REPORTER ABOUT GAZA POSTS
The article came days after Accurso accused celebrities who haven't spoken out about Gaza of having a racial double standard in how they value children.
"They probably would say something if these kids were White and from a different place. Please stop being racist and risk something," Accurso said on Instagram.
She was also one of several prominent progressives who called out singer Ed Sheeran following Macklemore's removal as the opening act for his tour after he repeatedly called for a "Free Palestine" and performed his anti-Israel song "Hind's Hall" during his act.
"Ed Sheeran had an opportunity [to] show that we won't be bullied into punishing people for supporting Palestine. Instead, he caved to people who refuse to accept what the world knows. A genocide is happening in Gaza. We all need to speak out against it," Accurso wrote.
"If more than 20,000 White children were killed in another part of the world, everyone would be shouting about it at their concerts," she added. "Treating some children's lives as less worthy of outrage is racist. Silence during a genocide is not neutral."
MS RACHEL CONFRONTED ON ACCUSING ISRAEL OF 'GENOCIDE' IN PARK INTERACTION WITH PODCASTER
Accurso has been criticized by pro-Israel organizations and groups that say her posts have shared anti-Israel propaganda by repeatedly accusing the Jewish nation of committing "genocide."
Rabbi Yaakov Menken, the executive vice president of the Coalition for Jewish Values, said in a statement to Fox News Digital, "To attempt to dress up Jew-hatred as a righteous cause is by no means new. No one is criticizing Rachel Accurso because she doesn't 'want kids to be killed and starved.'"
"She claims to care about 35.5 million children suffering from acute malnutrition across Africa, the Middle East, and Asia, but spends an inordinate amount of time speaking about 0.031 million children in Gaza," he added. "When 0.09% of starving children receive 90% of her attention, something is wrong."
"She had nothing to say about Israeli children being held hostage until seven months later, when the backlash became too loud to ignore. It is clear that her problem is not a deep concern for children, but that she is using her purported deep concern to mask something much darker," Menken concluded.

titulo: Lost in translation: Israel, Huckabee blast Macron over Hamas comments as France clarifies wording
texto_limpo:
President Donald Trump offered a roaring counterbalance to a spate of world leaders bashing Israel or appearing to equivocate between the October 7 Hamas terror attacks and Jerusalem's response - as one world leader was assailed for his comments on Hamas.
Gaza dominated the opening day of the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday, despite a ceasefire, as world leaders accused Israel of continuing to displace Palestinians and undermine prospects for peace.
French President Emmanuel Macron accused Israel of violating Palestinian rights in the West Bank, questioning the justification for its actions and making a remark that was translated as "Hamas was never active in the West Bank."
MIDDLE EAST TAKES CENTER STAGE AT UN AS REGIONAL LEADERS CONFRONT IRAN WAR, GAZA AND HOUTHI THREAT
Israeli U.N. Ambassador Danny Danon challenged his claim about Hamas' presence in the West Bank. "French President Emmanuel Macron claimed from the UN podium that Hamas has 'never been active' in Judea and Samaria. Just two days ago, a French citizen was murdered there," Danon wrote on X. "Mr. President, Emmanuel Macron, do your homework before lecturing Israel. Check the facts."
Asked by Fox News Digital to clarify Macron's remarks, a French Foreign Ministry spokesperson said: "The president meant to say that Hamas does not govern the West Bank. His remarks should therefore not be misinterpreted."
In response to the comments, U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee reposted Israel's Minister of Diaspora and Combating Antisemitism. Huckabee stated, "Hard to imagine a more out of touch with reality speech than Macron at UN. corrects the record. Hamas is an evil scourge, and they have killed innocent American citizens.
Chickli's post noted in part that, "Since 1990, Hamas has carried out more than 80 lethal terrorist attacks originating in or directed from Judea and Samaria, murdering more than 350 Israeli civilians." Judea and Samaria is another term used for the West Bank.
Macron also accused Israel of violating Palestinian rights in the West Bank and undermining the sovereignty of neighboring Lebanon, where he said villages in the south were being "razed." Macron questioned the credibility of the international community's recognition of Palestinian statehood if it failed to act on the situation in Gaza. "Some claim that peace has been achieved," he said, calling the situation "shameful."
U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, in his final address to the U.N. General Assembly (UNGA) as secretary-general, opened fire on Israel's response in Gaza, describing it as "a scale of killing and destruction unlike anything I have witnessed in all my years as Secretary-General."
"Amid the turmoil engulfing the region, we must not lose sight of the devastating situation in the Occupied Palestinian Territory," he said, as the world approaches three years since the Hamas terror attacks that sparked the Israeli military response he spent much of his speech criticizing.
At the same time, Guterres lamented the ongoing conflict in Sudan, saying the war-torn East African nation is a place the "world looks away" from wrongly.
Yet his decision to single out Gaza as "the worst" devastation he had witnessed during his tenure raised questions about the international community's uneven attention to two of the world's deadliest conflicts. Approximately 72,000 Palestinians have been reported killed in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run Health Ministry, compared with an estimated 150,000 people killed in Sudan's civil war. Many of those killed in Gaza include terrorists.
King Abdullah II of Jordan, a regional U.S. ally whose country signed a peace agreement with Israel in 1994, doubled down on the anti-Israel tenor, accusing Jerusalem of "war crimes."
"In my region, from Lebanon to Yemen, to Sudan, protracted conflict is deepening humanitarian suffering," Abdullah said. "And if anyone had any doubt that a crisis in our part of the world stays there, just look at the energy and grocery bills of ordinary families, from Mumbai to Madrid to Minnesota."
WORLD LEADERS DESCEND ON NEW YORK FOR UNGA - BUT WHO REALLY HAS AMERICA'S EAR?
Abdullah said Jordanian field hospitals had been targeted during the first 300 days of the "so-called ceasefire" and lamented the deaths of Palestinian children.
He also praised Trump for "pushing hard for peace" while pivoting to fault Israel for "moving the goalposts" and allegedly destroying civilian infrastructure in Gaza.
"The question is, is this the behavior of a democratic state governed by law? What is unfolding across the West Bank is not a series of isolated acts. It is elements of a single policy to compel an entire population to leave their land," Abdullah said.
"And there is a name for that: forced displacement. And that is a war crime."
Abdullah also accused Israel of harboring territorial ambitions in Syria, calling on the international community to act.
Just before Abdullah, President Donald Trump offered a scathing counterweight to the invective directed at the Netanyahu administration and Israel's response to Palestinian terrorism.
BRITAIN'S DRAMATIC CRACKDOWN ON ISRAELI SETTLEMENTS SPARKS FIERCE RESPONSE AS US BLOWBACK LOOMS
"Iran will never have a nuclear weapon" was a mantra repeated by Trump from the dais, as he noted that the Khamenei regime had also celebrated October 7 as a "service to humanity" while murdering thousands of Iranian citizens in recent months, according to the president.
"Just imagine such a vile regime, wherever empowered to carry out large-scale terror attacks from behind a nuclear shield. This was the reality we had to confront, the reality that far too many preferred to ignore," he said, taking occasional swipes at nations - and previous U.S. leaders - who refused to help neutralize the Iranian threat.
"Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?" he asked. "But I believe we'll make a deal right after the election," he added, suggesting Iran is waiting to see whether Republicans retain control of Congress while noting that he himself is not on the ballot.
Meanwhile, criticism of Israel continued from the dais throughout the day.
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva said that former Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and former Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat were "statesmen" who sought solutions with courage and clarity.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
"They were defeated by hatred," Lula da Silva claimed, according to the U.N.'s transcript of his remarks.
"Generations of Palestinians will carry the pain and trauma left by the genocide of women and children perpetrated by Netanyahu['s] government in Gaza," he said.
Danon told Fox News Digital that, "Unfortunately, it's not new, but the U.N. is obsessed with Israel."
"Instead of focusing and dealing with the real issues, they all gather and gang against Israel," he said. "[It is] the weakness of the secretary general. That is why we are grateful for President Trump, who came to the U.N., delivered a very powerful speech with moral clarity, but we are used to it... Unfortunately, instead of taking practical actions to improve the world, it's much easier to blame Israel about everything," he said.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, called Gaza "the world's biggest graveyard for children" and compared the situation there to Holocaust-era concentration camps, continuing his history of comparing Israel to Nazi Germany.
Danon said it is legitimate to criticize Israel and that its leaders welcome debate - but that the U.N. instead delved into "pure hate [and] incitement," singling out Erdoğan, who is supposed to be a Western ally.
"[He] comes here every year, compares the Israelis to the Nazis. That's shameful. That's shameful. And he shows that he's an antisemite. He doesn't really care about the Palestinians. He just wants to sow chaos and instigate against the Jewish people."
As for King Abdullah's remarks, Danon said, "He should know better. We work with Jordan, we support Jordan, we defended Jordan in the past. But unfortunately, many leaders, when they come here, they don't speak about the cooperation with Israel, the economical or security cooperation. They join the group and they always criticize us."

titulo: Top Democrat survives double-barreled challenge as party’s Israel divide hits home
texto_limpo:
House Democratic Whip Katherine Clark toppled two progressive challengers Tuesday in Massachusetts' safely Democratic 5th Congressional District, surviving a primary fight that put Gaza and pro-Israel political spending at the center of the race.
Clark, who won handily Tuesday night against fellow Democratic Party contenders Jonathan Paz and Tarik Samman, was first elected in 2013 during a special election and has held her position as House Democratic whip since 2022.
The second-highest ranking Democrat after House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Clark has helped lead opposition to Republican spending, immigration and healthcare measures, including recent messaging against ICE funding and GOP cuts to Head Start and Medicaid.
MEET THE FAR-LEFT INSURGENTS WAGING WAR ON THE DEMOCRATIC ESTABLISHMENT IN 2026 MIDTERMS
She ran against former city councilor, educator and union organizer Paz and 27-year-old Harvard Law School researcher and union organizer Samman.
Clark fended off two left-wing challengers who sought to make Gaza and pro-Israel political money central issues in the safely blue Boston-area primary.
Her fundraising operation dwarfed both challengers, raising $4.5 million, while Paz raised $88,500 and Samman brought in $43,800, according to FEC filings.
PELOSI-BACKED DEMOCRAT LOSES AFTER $10M FLOOD OF CRYPTO, PRO-ISRAEL MONEY
While AIPAC, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, endorsed Clark and has contributed to her campaign in the past, she has taken a critical stance toward the Israeli government's handling of the war in Gaza.
AIPAC is an influential pro-Israel lobbying group that has been criticized for advocating for U.S. military aid to Israel amid the war in Gaza.
Last year, Clark used the word "genocide" at a district event before clarifying that she was not accusing Israel of genocide. Then, in July, she voted to cut $3.3 billion in U.S. military aid, saying Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government had failed to meet U.S. interests and values.
Clark has continued to support Israel as a sovereign Jewish state and backed U.S. assistance for some Israeli defensive systems but is critical of Netanyahu.
TOP HOUSE DEMOCRAT SAYS ANTI-ISRAEL ACTIVISTS' THREATS KEPT HIM FROM TOWN HALLS FOR A YEAR
Samman and Paz have argued that while Clark has increasingly criticized Israel's conduct in Gaza, she has yet to renounce the AIPAC money she has accepted.
Clark ran unopposed in 2024. Her most recent general election opponent was Republican Caroline Colarusso, whom Clark defeated 74% to 26% in 2022.

titulo: New York Times faces shareholder lawsuit over alleged anti-Israel bias
texto_limpo:
New York Times shareholders filed a lawsuit Wednesday against the paper's parent company, demanding that its board hand over internal records concerning how it has handled topics, including the Israel-Hamas war.
The State Board of Administration of Florida (SBA) and conservative nonprofit National Center for Public Policy Research (NCPPR) filed the petition in New York County Supreme Court, seeking to compel The New York Times Company to produce internal records showing how the board oversees editorial standards, fact-checking, corrections, source verification, defamation exposure and reputational risk, with the paper's Gaza coverage being central to the shareholders' concerns.
The petition claimed that The New York Times has had a recent history of "materially false or baseless factual assertions," citing a peer-reviewed study published in 2024 that found the Times admitted 72 errors in its Israel-Hamas war coverage between <DATE> and <DATE>, with 48 of these errors about Israel, and that the "[c]orrections were late, vague and sometimes evasive."
"The Company's repeated publication of materially false or baseless factual assertions, many later admitted internally or disproven externally, supports a reasonable inference that the Board has not only failed in its obligation to monitor the Company's internal controls, but it has allowed such flagrantly selective application of the internal controls to support the conclusion that in the absence of any Board-level oversight, journalistic standards have been weaponized within the Company to serve the personal agendas of unchecked editors," the petition read.
NEW YORK TIMES LOSES DEFAMATION SUIT, ORDERED TO PAY $9.25M TO FORMER ALABAMA BASKETBALL PLAYER
"That inference is strengthened by what Petitioners' investigation did not find: any Board-level committee, independent oversight function, or other objective third party charged with assessing whether the Company effectively enforces and complies with its own editorial standards," the complaint continued.
"Put plainly, although the Company adopted certain internal journalistic controls (including controls against biased reporting and misreporting), Petitioners found no indication that the Board established any mechanism for information about compliance with those controls to reach the Board," it added.
"Making matters worse, numerous instances of gross violations of those controls were brought to the attention of Board members who double as Company executives, yet the Board seemingly refused to take any corrective or protective action."
The petition cites a <DATE>, opinion column by Nicholas Kristof titled "The Silence That Meets the Rape of Palestinians," whose sourcing and claims, the shareholders allege, were publicly criticized and "shown to be exaggerated, manipulated, and unsupported."
The petition also claimed that The New York Times fostered an unwelcoming environment for differences of opinion, citing a whistleblower who raised concerns about anti-Israel bias in the paper's reporting with Human Resources and was allegedly told, "If you don't like our values here, maybe you should go find a place whose values align with yours."
The New York Times has, according to the petition, rejected prior demands for the requested records, saying the demand "does not serve a proper purpose and violates the First Amendment" and that the petitioners' concerns are "transparently pretextual and made in bad faith" as well as saying the demands "are improper on their face because they seek records of the day-to-day business and editorial judgments of The Times" and qualify as "coordinated harassment."
A spokesperson for the Times dismissed the lawsuit in comments to Fox News Digital.
"This lawsuit has no merit and was brought for an improper purpose," the paper said in a statement. "Although it is positioned as a corporate governance petition to inspect the company's books and records, it is a transparent attempt to exert agenda-driven pressure against an independent media organization, level false allegations of bias and chill journalism protected by the First Amendment. We will defend against the suit vigorously."
Gerard Filitti, senior counsel with The Lawfare Project, a Jewish civil and human rights organization, described the case in more detail in comments to Fox News Digital.
"In May, The Lawfare Project sent The New York Times a seven-page retraction demand on the [Nicholas] Kristof column, documenting that the column's primary source is chaired by a man on Israel's list of Hamas operatives who called the October 7 attackers 'heroic knights,' and that its validating expert left UCLA amid sexual harassment allegations involving minors," Filitti said.
"The Times' deputy general counsel answered that he saw 'no basis for a retraction or correction' because the story 'was carefully edited and fact-checked.' Yet less than two months later, the paper's executive editor said the newsroom 'wouldn't have done that exact piece,'" he continued.
"Shortly after our demand, the paper's own shareholders asked a narrower question - whether anyone above the editors checks that the Times follows its own written standards - and the Times refused to even provide them with the charters and standards handbook it already publishes.
"The petition filed today puts the Times' credibility in front of a judge, along with a record the paper has refused to answer anywhere else: 72 errors the paper admitted in eight months of war coverage, 48 of them about Israel; a front-page caption calling a Gaza child 'born healthy' that the paper walked back five days later; a columnist who quoted his own campaign donors in at least a dozen columns without telling readers; a 10-year Jewish employee told by Human Resources, according to the petition, to 'go find a place whose values align with yours;' and a federal jury that found the Times liable for defamation on <DATE>, the paper's first loss at trial in more than fifty years," Filitti added.
"This record comes from the Times' own corrections column, its own personnel and a jury, and it is now a court filing in New York County," he continued. "For the first time, the Times has to give an answer - in sworn papers, to a judge, on a public docket. The likely response, from a paper that sells credibility for a living, is that its own shareholders may not ask how it protects that credibility. The petition is a first step toward accountability, and a larger one toward public recognition that the problem is systemic."

titulo: Hamas slams Board of Peace for refusal to work with UNRWA in Gaza
texto_limpo:
Hamas slams Board of Peace for refusal to work with UNRWA in Gaza
Hamas accuses Board of Peace of aligning with Israel after excluding UN agency for Palestinians from Gaza operations.
Palestinian group Hamas has condemned the Board of Peace's decision not to work with the United Nations agency for Palestinians, UNRWA, and for saying that the agency will have no role in Gaza.
The US-created Board's decision is "a complete alignment with the Zionist [Israeli] position", aimed at ending UNRWA's operations, preventing it from delivering aid to Palestinians and eliminating the right of return, Hamas spokesperson Hazem Qassem said on Saturday.
On Friday, the Board of Peace said that "UNRWA's involvement in Gaza is unchanged."
"We will only work with trusted partners who will deliver for the people of Gaza and contribute to a deradicalized Strip," it said in a post on X, adding that "UNRWA fails on those litmus tests".
In his statement, Qassem said it was "strange for the Peace Council to adopt this hostile stance towards UNRWA while simultaneously failing to provide aid to Gaza or compel the occupation to abide by the ceasefire agreement and halt the daily killings of Palestinians in the Strip".
UNRWA, set up in 1949, has for decades provided aid and education services to Palestinian refugees and preserved their national rights.
Palestinians see the agency as safeguarding their right of return to their homeland, while Israel wants it dismantled.
'UNRWA's days are over'
The Associated Press reported on Friday that Board of Peace members had been more willing to work with UNRWA behind the scenes than their public stance suggested.
At the Board of Peace briefing to the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, officials named several UN agencies as partners. UNRWA was not among them.
However, a Board of Peace official, speaking to The AP on condition of anonymity, confirmed that board members had met UNRWA officials several times.
The official said the agency's programmes could continue if they served Gaza's residents well, but maintained that "UNRWA's days are over".
Philippe Lazzarini, who led UNRWA until earlier this year, told The AP that members of the Palestinian technocratic committee appointed by the Board to govern Gaza wanted to work with the agency.
On Thursday, Lazzarini accused the Board of failing to deliver on its mandate, saying in a post on X that Israeli authorities are still blocking basic aid "as part of a wider plan to keep Gaza unlivable for Palestinians".
"Grandiose plans is what the Board of Peace does best. Plans however will not keep the people of Gaza warm this winter," he added, urging that crossings into Gaza be opened and supplies let in at scale.
Gaza, West Bank attacks continue
On the ground on Saturday, Israel's pattern of violations against Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank continued.
Israeli attacks killed seven Palestinians across the Gaza Strip in the past 48 hours, including one person who succumbed to wounds sustained prior, Gaza's Ministry of Health said.
In northern Gaza, Israeli forces shot dead a Palestinian in Jabalia, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported. An Israeli drone strike near Joulis Street and al-Nouri Tower in the Nuseirat refugee camp killed another person and wounded others.
In al-Mawasi in Khan Younis, an Israeli drone strike wounded several Palestinians, including a girl, while Israeli artillery shelled areas east of the city.
An Israeli quadcopter also opened fire on Salah al-Din Street in central Gaza, wounding three people, including another girl.
Meanwhile, in the occupied West Bank, Israeli forces stormed Ramallah-based Birzeit University, raiding one of its buildings while students sat final examinations, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.
In Tulkarem, forces arrested resident Bashar Odeh after raiding his home in Shuweika, and interrogated others during home searches in Zeita.
In Bethlehem governorate, Israeli forces closed the military gates at the entrances to western villages, stopping residents, including pedestrians, from passing.
Raids continued across other localities, including the Qalandiya and Am'ari refugee camps.

titulo: The pro-Israel censors are starting to lose
texto_limpo:
The pro-Israel censors are starting to lose
The Macklemore controversy demonstrates that the cost of speaking up for Palestine is diminishing.
For decades, Israel's greatest advantage in the West was not simply military or political support. It was narrative power.
Israel and its supporters enjoyed enormous influence over the boundaries of acceptable discussion about Palestine: which violent incident received attention, whose security mattered the most, which historical context was relevant and, crucially, what criticism of Israel could be allowed in public.
That power has not disappeared. But the extraordinary controversy surrounding Macklemore's removal from Ed Sheeran's US tour shows how rapidly it is eroding.
The fact that the American rapper was dropped from the tour after he spoke about Palestine on stage meant that the old system worked. A powerful billionaire objected. Venues applied pressure. The artist disappeared from the stage.
What was different this time was the backlash.
In response to the censorship, every remaining support act on Sheeran's tour walked away. Finneas, Lukas Graham, Aaron Rowe and Beoga all withdrew. Meanwhile, ticket prices for Sheeran's remaining concerts plunged, in some cases losing 50 percent of their value, as many fans felt outraged.
Macklemore stood his ground and pledged the $1m he had earned from his appearances to six organisations supporting Palestinians. Subsequently, the media reported Sheeran would donate $2m towards humanitarian relief in the region.
All of this has helped generate further donations and attention for Palestinian aid organisations, including a $1m pledge from children's educator Ms Rachel.
Consider what happened.
An attempt to push "Free Palestine" off the stage resulted in Palestine receiving vastly more attention, artists abandoning one of the world's biggest tours and more funds being donated to Palestinian organisations.
The attempt to control the message amplified the message itself. And that tells us something much bigger than how controversy is handled in the music industry.
Amid its genocide in Gaza, Israel is facing a crisis not simply of public opinion, but of narrative control.
For almost three years, the world has watched Palestinians killed, displaced and starved. It has seen neighbourhoods flattened, hospitals overwhelmed and families repeatedly driven from one place to another. A United Nations Commission of Inquiry has concluded that Israel committed genocide in Gaza. The International Criminal Court has issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.
The old narrative increasingly struggles against a force Israel cannot easily control: people can see what is happening themselves.
Palestinian journalists, doctors, parents and ordinary citizens no longer depend entirely on Western governments or established media organisations to narrate their lives. Images, testimony and documentation travel directly from Gaza to millions of phones around the world.
There are limits to propaganda when people can witness the consequences of power for themselves. Public opinion increasingly reflects that rupture.
A Pew Research Center survey across 36 countries this year found a median of 67 percent of respondents held an unfavourable view of Israel. In the United Kingdom, it was 69 percent, Germany - 73 percent, Italy - 75 percent and Australia - 79 percent. Even in the United States, Israel's most important ally, 60 percent viewed Israel unfavourably.
Among younger people, the transformation is more dramatic still. Seventy-four percent of Americans aged 18 to 34 surveyed by Pew viewed Israel unfavourably, as did 78 percent of young Britons and 87 percent of young Australians.
This does not mean everyone supports Palestine or agrees on what a political settlement should look like. It means that the cost of speaking up for Palestine is falling.
For years, the implied question confronting artists, academics and other public figures openly supporting Palestine was: what are you prepared to lose? Your booking? Your sponsorship? Your reputation? Your career?
The purpose of such consequences was larger than the individual. Punish one person publicly and hundreds of others would understand the warning and keep silent.
But deterrence only works when people are deterred.
This time, they weren't. And that put pressure on the censors and those who complied.
The backlash forced Sheeran to speak up publicly about Palestine. On Saturday, during his concert in Philadelphia, where he had to play solo, he called what is happening in Gaza "unjustifiable".
The equation has clearly changed.
Speaking for Palestine can still carry a professional cost. Macklemore has just demonstrated that. But increasingly, censors may discover that silencing pro-Palestine voices carries a cost, too.
That is why the Israeli narrative crisis runs deeper than falling approval ratings.
The old power was not merely the ability to silence Palestinians and those who stood with them. It was the ability to determine which account of Palestine the world would hear. That monopoly is breaking.
They succeeded in removing the man who said "Free Palestine" from the stage. But "Free Palestine" became louder.
And that may be the clearest indication yet that Israel is not simply losing an argument. It is losing its grip on the story.

Qatar is holding talks with Oman and Pakistan to de-escalate tensions in the region, the country's Foreign Ministry has said, after a recent flare-up in fighting between the US and Iran.
Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed Al-Ansari warned on Tuesday against normalising the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, where the war between Iran and the US has seen shipping in the waterway grind almost to a halt.
"We said from the start, any attempt to normalise the closure of the Strait of Hormuz in this way will end with regional escalation, and this is what we saw yesterday and today," Al-Ansari said in the press conference.
"Escalation does not benefit anyone, and we are all negatively impacted by the escalation. We encourage all sides to be wise and return to negotiations."
Around 25 percent of the world's seaborne trade passed through the strait before Israel and the US launched a war on Iran on <DATE>, reducing traffic in the waterway to a trickle.
The US has enforced a blockade on Iranian ports, while Iran has been accused of laying mines and attacking tankers in the waterway. Energy prices have since skyrocketed, affecting economies across the world.
Iran and Oman have held talks on opening a temporary route through the Strait of Hormuz, but Tehran wants the US to first return to a memorandum of understanding agreed in June.
Qatar, which has been economically impacted by the war, has encouraged a peaceful resolution to the crisis and is in contact with regional leaders to encourage dialogue, Al-Ansari said.
Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani visited Tehran last week to encourage dialogue to end the crisis.
"The [regional] visits [to Tehran]... are all to support mediation efforts, and attempting to return to the negotiation path, and guaranteeing no return to escalation in the region," Al-Ansari said about the visit.
"During his visit [the Qatari Prime Minister] confirmed Qatar's consistent position in support of diplomatic efforts to find a solution to this crisis... efforts are ongoing."

Recent weeks have also seen a spike in pogroms by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank, with Palestinian homes and villages besieged.
Al-Ansari accused Israel of using the war on Iran "to impose a new reality in Palestinian, Lebanese and Syrian territories" and accused it of beginning a new regional escalation.

titulo: UK charities, protest groups condemn Israeli ban threat after sanctions
texto_limpo:
UK charities, protest groups condemn Israeli ban threat after sanctions
Having warned London of 'consequences' for sanctions, Israel targets UK charities, campaign groups and Palestine Action.
London, United Kingdom - British charities, Palestinian advocacy organisations and the proscribed Palestine Action group have condemned an official Israeli letter maligning their representatives and activists and recommending they be barred from entering Israel.
The document, seen by Al Jazeera, was issued by Israel's Ministry for Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism. It recommends border authorities bar employees and activists associated with aid organisations including Oxfam, Islamic Relief Worldwide, Save the Children, Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP) and the Norwegian Refugee Council, which receives UK funding, as well as campaign groups including the Palestine Solidarity Campaign and Friends of Al-Aqsa.
The letter, dated <DATE>, the day the UK banned imports from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, was previously reported by the BBC and Jerusalem Post.
Ismail Patel, founder of Friends of Al-Aqsa, which openly advocates for the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement, is accused in the letter of joining anti-Israel demonstrations in London and making "harsh statements against Israel" in public appearances and interviews.
"To hear Israel is planning to ban Friends of Al-Aqsa for our BDS campaign clearly shows BDS is working and impacting Israel," Patel told Al Jazeera. "Israeli restrictions will not intimidate us."
Israel's Diaspora Affairs Ministry did not respond to Al Jazeera's request for comment.
Israel follows through on threat of 'consequences'
Israel had warned the UK against the new sanctions, with its Ministry of Foreign Affairs raising the prospect of "consequences" for what it called "hostile moves".
Shortly after the trade ban was announced, Israel, which controls access to Gaza and the occupied West Bank, barred 11 British MPs and a lawyer from entering and ordered the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem. It also announced the removal of British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center located in Kiryat Gat, southern Israel. And it has ended British training of Palestinian Authority forces in the occupied West Bank.
"In light of this [the trade ban], attention should be directed to the ongoing and subversive activities of various British organisations promoting boycotts, sanctions, and economic and political measures against the State of Israel," the leaked letter reads.
It makes further accusations against 11 groups in total. The claims against them range from advocating for engagement with Hamas for humanitarian access; demanding an arms embargo against Israel; having ties to the Muslim Brotherhood or working with "terrorist" organisations.
Save the Children is accused of describing Israel's actions as "deliberate starvation" and "genocide".
A spokesperson told Al Jazeera that, alongside other NGOs, it is already unable to secure visas for staff needing to cross Israeli-controlled borders into Gaza or the West Bank, "at a time when needs have never been greater".
Israel has intensified restrictions on international aid groups since the genocidal war in Gaza began, including measures affecting the entry of food, medicine, foreign volunteer doctors and humanitarian workers.
MAP said the letter forms part of Israeli authorities' "wider restrictions on international charities operating in the occupied Palestinian territory". It noted that two MAP individuals named in the letter had received the humanitarian medals awarded by King Charles.
The letter describes Palestine Action, which has carried out raids against Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit Systems, as a "network of radical branches promoting direct action intended to damage the Israeli defence industry".
"This letter is further proof that we were not banned because of anything to do with 'terrorism'," Palestine Action cofounder Huda Ammori told Al Jazeera. "As the letter admits, our activity was always focused on damaging the Israeli defence industry."
In a related development, UK Lawyers for Israel has called on the government to consider proscribing Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF, as a terrorist organisation, The Telegraph reported. The lobby group alleged, in line with Israeli accusations, that MSF had employed people with links to Palestinian armed groups.
