titulo: Israel faces mounting diplomatic pressure ahead of Netanyahu’s UN address
texto_limpo:
Israel faces mounting diplomatic pressure ahead of Netanyahu's UN address
Trade measures targeting Israeli settlements and growing criticism over Gaza show signs of a widening divide between Israel and some of its Western allies.
BRUSSELS: Israel is facing growing diplomatic pressure at this year's United Nations General Assembly, as some of its closest Western allies take a tougher stance over Gaza and Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is showing little sign of backing down.
Netanyahu has said he would defend Israel's military actions against the Palestinians at the UN this week. He is slated to speak at the General Assembly on Thursday (<DATE>) evening.
"I'm coming to the UN," Netanyahu said in a video statement on Tuesday. "I'm going to tell the truth about our heroic soldiers."
Nearly 130 heads of state and government are attending the UN's High-level Week in New York, with the General Debate running from Tuesday (<DATE>) to <DATE>.
For Israel, this year's gathering comes against a markedly different diplomatic backdrop.
Ahead of last year's gathering, several Western countries with longstanding ties to Israel, including the United Kingdom, Canada and Australia, formally recognised Palestinian statehood, marking a break with longstanding policy.
France did the same at a high-level conference at the UN in New York.
A year later, as the Gaza war approaches its third year, Israel finds itself increasingly isolated on the international stage.
Public opinion of Israel has deteriorated in many countries, according to a Pew Research Center survey this year. The findings showed that across 36 countries, a median of 67 per cent of adults had an unfavourable view of Israel.
PRESSURE OVER WEST BANK SETTLEMENTS
The Israeli government's support for settlement expansion in the West Bank has also prompted concern and condemnation from some of its closest allies.
On <DATE>, the foreign ministers of 12 countries, including the UK and France, said they would support or consider restrictions on trade in goods with Israeli settlements in the West Bank that are illegal under international law.
The move marked a toughening of the Britain's stance on Israel under new Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Britain's Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who took up the post in July, also criticised settler violence, saying the UK believed there is "ethnic cleansing" of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank.
"Today we refuse to be bystanders to further suffering and to the destruction of the two-state solution," Miliband said.
Kaja Kallas, the European Union's High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy and Vice-President of the European Commission, said: "Settler violence against Palestinians continues to rise, and too often goes unchecked.
"The E1 settlements will further undermine the prospect of the two-state solution by driving a wedge through the West Bank."
But the EU's 27 member states remain divided over taking tougher action against Israel.
Countries such as Spain and Ireland have pushed for punitive measures, while getting countries that have historically maintained closer ties with Israel, such as Germany, on board has proven more difficult.
NETANYAHU NOT BACKING DOWN
The Israeli prime minister has made it clear the country will not bend to international pressure, particularly when it comes to Gaza and its position on Hamas.
"The IDF (Israel Defense Forces) will continue to thwart the threats against our forces and our citizens, because once again, the existence of Israel and the security of all the citizens of Israel are not up for negotiation," Netanyahu said in August.
There have also been signs of tension between Israel and its most important ally, the United States, after it refused to withdraw from Lebanon - one of Iran's conditions in the memorandum of understanding with the US in June to end their conflict.
This did not go down well in the Trump administration.
"Donald J. Trump is the only head of state in the entire world who is sympathetic to the nation of Israel at this moment in time," said US Vice President JD Vance in June.
"If I was in the cabinet of the Israeli government, I might not be attacking the only powerful ally that I have anywhere left in the entire world."
US-ISRAEL TIES
Despite such tensions, experts say the longstanding ties between Israel and the US remain intact.
Elisa Ewers, senior fellow for Middle East studies at American think-tank, the Council on Foreign Relations, said disagreements between the two governments have not fundamentally altered the relationship.
"We see these momentary revelations of tensions but the underlying foundation in the relationship, especially between the two presidents, is still very much there," said Ewers.
"So, the question becomes, how does this affect ... election cycles in both countries?"
The US is heading into midterm elections on <DATE>, with opinion polls suggesting that Democrats could wrest control of the Senate from Republicans, many of whom have maintained strong support for Netanyahu.
For Israel, analysts say its government's position is unlikely to soften ahead of October's general election, particularly as Netanyahu seeks to bolster his reputation as a defender of Israel.
Oliver McTernan, director of Forward Thinking, a UK-based charity that deals with conflict resolution, said opposition to Palestinian statehood remained strong among Israeli voters.
"A good 70 per cent of the Israeli population would be in empathy with Netanyahu's plan to finish the job," said McTernan.
"They'll say: 'We'll never feel secure if we go back to what the situation was before, or if we have a Palestinian state'."
Sanctions and diplomatic rebukes may increase the pressure on Israel as it faces growing criticism from countries with which it has traditionally had close ties.
But whether they will lead to substantive impact on Israel's foreign policy remains uncertain.
With an election approaching, observers say the government's next moves are likely to be shaped as much by domestic voters as the international community.

titulo: Israel denounces 'grotesque absurdity' of Macron UN remarks on West Bank
texto_limpo:
Israel denounces 'grotesque absurdity' of Macron UN remarks on West Bank
JERUSALEM: Israel shot back angrily Tuesday (<DATE>) at French President Emmanuel Macron, who criticised Israeli actions in the West Bank by saying Hamas was not active in the territory that is home to the Palestinian Authority.
"The grotesque absurdity of Emmanuel Macron's statement is staggering," said a statement by the office of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is expected to deliver a defiant address to the world body on Thursday.
"Hamas terrorists carry out attacks against Jews almost every day. They have murdered countless Israeli civilians in Judea and Samaria," it said, using the Biblical name for the West Bank, which Israel seized in 1967.
Netanyahu's office pointed to the shooting death on Sunday, on the eve of Judaism's holiest day of Yom Kippur, of an Israeli settler in the West Bank. Israel said that the victim, father of six, Netanel Shukrun, also had French citizenship.
The Israeli military said it arrested the Palestinian gunman at a hospital and troops later raided his village. A minister in Netanyahu's government called for his execution under a new law.
Extremist Israeli settlers frequently attack and steal from West Bank Palestinians. The United Nations said there were about six settler-related violent incidents against Palestinians or their property daily through mid-2026 in the territory.
Macron, in his speech to the United Nations, deplored the humanitarian situation in Gaza - from which Hamas led the October 7 attack, the deadliest ever against Israel - as well as actions by Israel in the West Bank.
"What is our credibility worth if we remain inactive on Gaza? Some claim that peace has been achieved, but this has not opened up humanitarian deliveries. It is a spectacle that shames us all," Macron said.
"Look at what is happening in West Bank, where there are violations every day. In the name of what? Hamas has never struck in the West Bank. This every day makes it more impossible to achieve respect for the Palestinian people's legitimate right to exist."
The Palestinian Authority, led by Hamas's rivals, have semi-autonomy in major urban areas of the West Bank, with Israel controlling most of the territory.
Hamas took over Gaza in 2007, two years after Israel pulled out and dismantled settlements.
Netanyahu has poor relations with Macron, who led a push by Western nations at last year's UN General Assembly to recognise a Palestinian state.
France recently joined Britain in imposing sanctions on products from Israeli settlements in the West Bank, again angering the Israeli government.

titulo: Netanyahu faces backlash over report he was warned of Hamas attack days before October 7
texto_limpo:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faced a fierce political backlash Tuesday over a report that the president of the UAE had warned him of a major Hamas operation days before the October 7 attack.
The Prime Minister's Office dismissed the report as an "absolute lie." But with Israel's October elections less than two months away, Netanyahu's rivals seized on it as the latest evidence of what they say is a growing list of warnings he had ignored.
The four opposition party leaders - Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Avigdor Lieberman and Yair Golan - issued a rare joint statement calling for "an immediate and thorough investigation" into Netanyahu's "failures and malfunctioning."
"The Israeli public is entitled to know: What did Netanyahu know, when did he know, why he didn't update the security establishment, and why he didn't act to protect Israeli civilians?" the statement said.
Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett said the report is "true," writing on X that Netanyahu's alleged disregard for the warnings amounts to "criminal negligence." Bennett's political ally, former Prime Minister Yair Lapid, said he too had publicly warned of an attack before it happened, as had top Israeli security officials as well as Egyptian officials. "If Netanyahu had fulfilled his role, the massacre would have been prevented," Lapid said in a statement.
The report, published in the Haaretz newspaper, was based on findings from an upcoming book by Israeli journalists Shlomi Eldar and Ruti Yuval. It said UAE President Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed called Netanyahu about 10 days before October 7 and, during a 45-minute call, warned him that Hamas' Gaza leader Yahya Sinwar was planning a major move against Israel that could cause bloodshed and destabilize the region. The report cited a message Sinwar conveyed to the UAE and Israel through a Palestinian mediator in mid-<DATE>, warning of an upcoming "earthquake."
Haaretz reported that Netanyahu reacted "relatively calmly" to the information, and assured Bin Zayed that Israel was prepared for any scenario.
The UAE's Foreign Ministry issued a statement on Tuesday evening saying that it "does not comment on media stories or speculation regarding conversations between government leaders" but did not deny the call. "When necessary, all relevant intelligence has been and continues to be communicated between the relevant entities," the statement said.
An Israeli source familiar with the matter said Netanyahu's office had tried to get the UAE to deny the Haaretz report, but the UAE only agreed to put out a statement about intelligence sharing.
The Prime Minister's Office strongly denied the report, stating Netanyahu "did not speak with the president of the United Arab Emirates during the period in question and did not receive any warning from him."
Eldar, one of the journalists behind the report, pushed back on Netanyahu's denial of the report.
"It's true," he told CNN's Jake Tapper. "I worked on this report for almost a year and a half," he said.
"I have the document, I have records, I have everything that shows that the president of the UAE called Netanyahu a week an a half before October 7 and gave him a warning that Yahya Sinwar is planning a major attack on Israel," Eldar said.
Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu faces amplified political backlash over a report that the president of the UAE warned him of a major Hamas operation days before the October 7 attack. CNN's Oren Liebermann reports.
Accountability as an electoral issue
The report comes as Netanyahu's rivals work to make accountability for October 7 - the deadliest attack in Israel's history, during which over 1,200 people were murdered and more than 250 abducted to Gaza - a central campaign issue.
Netanyahu has now outlasted nearly every member of Israel's top security leadership from that day. Since the attack, the defense minister, the military chief of staff, and the directors of military intelligence, the Mossad and the Shin Bet, have all either resigned, been ousted, or reached the end of their terms.
Gadi Eisenkot, currently polling as Netanyahu's leading challenger, said the Haaretz report shows Netanyahu "led Israel blindly" toward the October 7 failures and renewed his pledge to establish a state commission of inquiry if elected.
Nearly three years after the attack, Netanyahu has resisted demands from bereaved families and October 7 survivors to establish an independent commission to investigate the security and intelligence failures that enabled Hamas to conduct the operation.
He and his associates have instead promoted a narrative blaming security chiefs for not waking him up the night before the attack despite intelligence indications that a Hamas offensive was imminent.
Last month, his wife, Sara Netanyahu, suggested that Yair Golan - a retired major general and the leader of the left-wing Democrats party who independently rushed to the Gaza border on October 7 to rescue survivors - had advance knowledge of the attack.
In an interview with the pro-government Channel 14, she questioned how Golan was "already dressed and ready" at dawn that day to head south, "while others knew nothing, including the prime minister."
Golan demanded an apology for what he called a "vile conspiracy theory" and said he would pursue a defamation suit, calling the allegation part of Netanyahu's attempt to "rewrite" the events of October 7 and deflect responsibility.
Following the Haaretz report, Golan wrote on X that the prime minister's "they-didn't-wake-me-up narrative is over. He knew, he was warned." He called it "not an error in judgment, but a conscious and criminal abandonment."
Hours later, the Democrats party sharpened its electoral campaign against Netanyahu, erecting a giant billboard over Tel Aviv's main highway bearing the headline: "The 1,200 murdered file - Causing death by negligence."

titulo: An ambassador in Ljubljana, but not in London: Israel’s foreign policy shifts away from longstanding allies
texto_limpo:
Gideon Saar smiled as he cut the blue ribbon outside the newly inaugurated embassy of Nauru in Jerusalem. Israel's foreign minister described the tiny Pacific island nation of some 12,000 people as "one of Israel's greatest friends in the international community."
Two days later, it was Slovenia's turn, as Saar cut the ribbon on a new embassy in Ljubljana. He praised the new center-right government for standing by Israel in the European Union, especially after the country had previously been one of Israel's harshest critics. A large business delegation was brought along to show appreciation.
There was no such celebration in London, where Israel faced one of its sharpest diplomatic rebukes in years: a coordinated move by the United Kingdom and 11 other countries to impose sanctions and trade restrictions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. Israel has had no ambassador in London for nearly a year. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's intended envoy, his chief of staff Tzachi Braverman, was barred from leaving Israel due to a criminal investigation, leaving the post vacant.
The split-screen moment reflects a broader pattern in Israel's foreign relations: As traditional partners in Western Europe grow distant, losing patience with the settlement expansion and surging violence in the West Bank, the right-wing government is cultivating ties with smaller or what it sees as more ideologically aligned countries, redirecting its diplomatic energy to other arenas.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband tied the new measures, announced in parliament on Tuesday, directly to Israel's decision to push ahead with the E1 settlement project, which critics say would cut the West Bank in two and close off the possibility of a contiguous future Palestinian state.
But the move is part of a longer-term shift. In <DATE>, Britain, Canada, France and more than a dozen other Western states recognized Palestinian statehood. And this June, the UK, Canada, France, Norway, Australia and New Zealand announced a wave of coordinated sanctions targeting individuals and networks accused of financing and enabling settler violence.
Some of the states announced additional punitive measures: France barred far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich from entering the country, Italy opened an investigation into National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir over the treatment of detained activists, including Italians, after Israel intercepted an aid flotilla on its way to Gaza. The Netherlands declared both Ben Gvir and Smotrich "persona non grata" and approved its own ban on imports of settlement goods.
Not every proposal has succeeded, and Israel has so far managed to stall broader actions from the EU. For years, Israel used Viktor Orban's government in Hungary to block EU measures. Now, following a change in leadership in Budapest, Slovenia has effectively taken Hungary's place as Israel's representative in Brussels. A push by France and Sweden for an EU ban on settlement trade was stalled, as were efforts to expel Israel from the EU's flagship Horizon research program.
Dr. Rémi Daniel, from Israel's Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) says the one comfort for Israel is that Germany and Italy have so far stuck to statements rather than joining the sanctions. "They are the most important EU member states because they have the power to block plans at the European level," he said.
But the trend was still concerning, he said, because looking at the balance of power within the EU, "the swinging center is going more against Israel."
Even as ties with some Western European allies fray, others are deepening their alliance with Israel through defense trade. Last month, Israel signed a $3.5 billion air-defense deal with Greece, one of the largest arm agreements in Israel's history. And in early 2026, Israel Aerospace Industries signed a $3.1 billion deal with Germany to expand its supply of Arrow missile interceptor systems.
Israel's response to the new sanctions - and its attitude towards one of its oldest allies in general - has been openly combative.
Saar swiftly announced he would close the British Consulate General in Jerusalem, end UK training for Palestinian Authority security forces, and ban entry to a dozen British officials and lawmakers. "The British move is morally distorted and constitutes a blatant interference in the affairs of a sovereign state and its electoral process," Saar said Tuesday.
Netanyahu labeled the UK the "Islamic Republic of Britain" on a podcast last month and has accused French President Emanuel Macron of fueling antisemitism by recognizing a Palestinian state.
While relations with some Western allies cool, and even the friendly Trump administration in the United States appears to be growingly frustrated with settler violence, Israel has been pouring energies into other regions and redrawing its map of relationships.
Declaring 2026 "The Year of South America," Saar has toured Argentina, Ecuador, Paraguay and Colombia and restored relations with Bolivia, Chile and Honduras. He also opened a communication channel with Venezuela for the first time since 2009, sending rescue teams to assist with earthquake relief last month.
New Israeli embassies opened in Zambia, Estonia, Moldova, Fiji and Slovenia. And Israel became the first country in the world to recognize the self-declared Republic of Somaliland as an independent state. Somaliland then opened an embassy in Jerusalem, where fewer than 10 countries have embassies, including the US. Argentina, Colombia, Costa Rica and the Democratic Republic of Congo have declared their intent to join the list.
Daniel Shek, a former Israeli ambassador to France, argues that this pivot comes at a real cost and says the government is damaging relationships built over decades on shared interests in economy, science, culture, security.
"They are sacrificing the alliances with the most significant countries," he said. "If Saar thinks the Paraguayan economy can replace France as a partner for export and import, good for him."
The countries involved in the sanctions, he said, are not ideologically hostile to Israel, just its actions under Netanyahu, Ben Gvir and Smotrich. "France, Britain, Italy, the Netherlands, are friendly countries fed up with this Israeli government's behavior."
Shek notes that the sanctions target the settlements, and not Israel itself, and that their practical bite, for now, is limited. Still, he says, they should not be underestimated.
"Once sanctions have been imposed, it is significant," he said. "There are things that have been opened and cannot be put back in the bottle."

titulo: Democrats might win in the midterms — but a whole new set of problems await
texto_limpo:
The left wing of the Democratic Party flourished this summer as fed-up liberals in key races across the country have eschewed traditional, more moderate candidates in favor of hard-charging progressives.
But behind the scenes, ultra-progressive House members and candidates are pushing their own party leaders to reflect more of that mood - arguing that Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries and his allies are, so far, failing to grasp the demands of far-left voters who showed up in droves this summer.
Those liberals watched in alarm in recent weeks as Jeffries publicly disavowed their marquee "Medicare for All" bill while a pro-Israel Democrat was elevated to a key foreign policy role within the caucus. They also argue his allies were working to undermine a pair of progressive candidates in Michigan and California.
"I was very confused and surprised by that," Rep. Pramila Jayapal, a senior progressive and author of the House's "Medicare for All" bill, told CNN about the leader's comments about her signature bill. She added that she has been having "direct" conversations with Jeffries about it.
The emerging frustrations on the left offer a preview of some of the pressures that await Jeffries if the party can flip the chamber next year, particularly as a new crop of far-left progressive candidates threaten not to support him for leader post-election.
"I think what we've seen around the country is that people all over are dissatisfied. They're not happy with the administration. They're not happy with the current leadership in the Democratic Party - and are looking for a change," Dr. Adam Hamawy, a progressive candidate who is likely to win a deep blue seat in New Jersey this November, told CNN. Hamawy is among several candidates fresh off primary victories who have not decided whether to back Jeffries.
"Most Democrats, I think, agree that the current leadership is failing to face the moment," Hamawy told CNN when asked if he'll support Jeffries. "I have to see what the choices are and what the situation is."
Tensions have long simmered within the Democratic Party, including in its fractious House caucus, where many centrists are privately pleased with what they see as Jeffries' effort to distance the party from a far-left agenda ahead of a critical election. But the rise of the democratic-socialist wing of the party has drawn new urgency to a major question now facing Jeffries: How much should the party embrace its insurgent left when it's also trying to win dozens of seats in GOP turf in November?
Nearly all progressives who spoke to CNN said Jeffries is still on track to become speaker next January if Democrats flip the chamber, according to conversations with more than a dozen Democrats. Privately, Jeffries has already met or made plans to meet with five of those insurgent Democrats: Hamawy in New Jersey, Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York, and Melat Kiros in Colorado, according to people familiar with the discussions.
Still, the recent frustrations on the left illustrate the challenge for Jeffries and his leadership team as they navigate the anti-establishment midterm mood within their party. The dissatisfaction goes beyond the upper echelons of leadership: there are preliminary internal discussions among current progressive members about challenging committee leaders and, possibly, instituting term limits for key roles, multiple people told CNN.
"Defeating 10, 30-year incumbents should be a wake-up call to the Democratic establishment that the base is moving underneath them," Usamah Andrabi, a spokesperson for a group helping to power the far-left wins, Justice Democrats, told CNN. (This cycle, nine of the group's endorsed candidates won primaries, its biggest year to date.)
Andrabi specifically pointed to Jeffries' comments on "Medicare for All" - in which Jeffries recently said he did not support the legislation: "Unfortunately, it often feels that the Democratic leadership and establishment don't even want to acknowledge the ground is moving."
Progressives, including Hamawy and Avila Chevalier, made clear in interviews with CNN they are coming to Washington to make real progress on an ambitious agenda on affordability and anti-corruption - not to simply antagonize leadership.
"We're not really going in to fight, we're going in to deliver on what people want," Hamawy said.
Yet even Jeffries' allies acknowledge the challenge awaiting him in January: navigating an intraparty battle over the party's ideological future. While an emboldened left wing is pushing for a major shake-up in Congress, Jeffries could also face an expanded centrist bloc that humiliated leadership last week when some of its members showed they were willing to defy the party line on key priorities - even if it meant helping Republicans.
That centrist rebellion has since triggered a messy internal feud among House Democrats. Privately, Jeffries and his team are discussing ways to crack down on any of their members voting for procedural motions that hurt the party - a proposal that has infuriated the left and centrists alike, according to Democrats from both factions.
A tense debate has since unfolded over whether party leaders should create new rules for next year to punish members who defy leadership. In a closed-door meeting on Wednesday about leadership's push, Progressive Caucus Chair Greg Casar of Texas pushed back firmly, arguing that members need to be able to voice dissent, according to multiple people familiar with the discussions. But he was immediately confronted by others, including Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz of Florida, who argued Democrats shouldn't be willing to go rogue on the floor.
Those dynamics will be on full display starting with the speaker's vote in January, if Democrats win the majority.
Avila Chevalier, a community organizer who shook New York City politics by unseating a long-time incumbent this summer, told CNN that she recently had a "positive" conversation with Jeffries.
But she said she hasn't "come to any final decisions on that yet," when asked whether she would support Jeffries as party leader, adding: "It'll be the first vote I make. It'll set the tone for the kind of representative that my district will have, and I want that vote to mean something to my community."
Even if many of the far-left incoming Democrats ultimately do support Jeffries, it's to their advantage not to show their cards just yet - creating what could be powerful leverage to negotiate for their priorities when they first arrive in Congress.
Asked more broadly about her agenda for next year, Avila Chevalier offered a range of "day one" priorities such as ending the sale of weapons to Israel, the Green New Deal for Public Housing and abolishing super PACs - as well as other ideas that are widely backed by the party like universal childcare and raising the minimum wage.
"It's time that folks who are in DC or elsewhere who might be comfortable with the status quo to recognize that the vast majority of the people of this country are hungry for something different," she said.
Angst over the emerging Democratic agenda
Many liberal Democrats are careful not to openly criticize their own leadership just ahead of a must-win midterm election.
But privately, progressive members and candidates remain concerned by Jeffries' comments publicly disavowing "Medicare for All" and saying he does not support the Democratic Socialists of America agenda in an interview last month with NBC's "Meet the Press."
Asked if he supports the bill, Jeffries said: "No, as you indicated, I haven't cosponsored the 'Medicare for All' legislation that has been introduced over the last several years," adding: "I do think we need to figure out how to fix our broken health care system and then build something better."
Jeffries' allies said his comments also reflect one of his long-time beliefs - that House leaders should not support major bills until there's broad support in the caucus.
Other progressives are concerned that party leaders are not adequately responding to the movement's vocal pro-Palestine push. They are, in particular, concerned about the recent elevation of prominent Israel supporter, Rep. Jared Moskowitz of Florida, to a Foreign Affairs subcommittee post that could give him influence over foreign policy next year.
Multiple Democrats told CNN that Jeffries was not involved in the move - saying instead that it was arranged by Rep. Brad Sherman, another Israel ally, who inherited the role after a colleague's resignation. Moskowitz, who's facing a tough reelection, asked Sherman if he could have the spot on the panel to help him with pro-Israel voters back home, those people said.
Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the Foreign Affairs Committee, dismissed the left's criticism, calling the hand-off "standard committee procedure." He added that Moskowitz had already held an important role on the committee - the top Democrat on the oversight subcommittee, which has since been passed off to Rep. Jonathan Jackson of Illinois.
"I don't know what the left's problem is," Meeks said, adding that he believes his committee is "very balanced" on the issue of Israel.
Still, the rise of Moskowitz has emerged as a major flashpoint among progressive lawmakers and candidates, especially after Jeffries had appealed to the left earlier this year by declaring that "American policy in the Middle East must change" after he opposed cutting taxpayer aid to Israel during a landmark vote earlier this year.
A 'shocking' intervention in California
Then there are party leaders' recent moves on the campaign trail.
In California, progressives are furious that their state's delegation leader, Rep. Zoe Lofgren, tried to tank a left-wing candidate in a bitter fight to fill the seat of former Rep. Eric Swalwell.
Progressive candidate, state Sen. Aisha Wahab, won the state party's endorsement and secured the most votes in two separate primaries for the seat (including a special election) - though she failed to top the 50 percent needed to avoid a runoff.
Ahead of that <DATE> runoff, Lofgren, a leadership ally, released a video statement questioning Wahab's fitness to serve in Congress and instead endorsed a more moderate candidate for the upcoming runoff.
The drama began after Lofgren and others, including No. 3 House Democrat Rep. Pete Aguilar, argued that California Democrats needed to fill the seat as quickly as possible and should install a "placeholder" Democrat to the seat temporarily.
But progressives argued Lofgren was simply trying to keep Wahab out of the role, giving the more moderate - and AIPAC-backed - candidate a better chance of winning a full term for the seat in November. (A person familiar with the subject said the congresswoman wasn't opposing her due to her progressive policy stands, but rather because of Wahab's refusal to back the push to install a "placeholder" Democrat to the seat through January.)
Wahab still won and was sworn into the House last week. But the cost, progressives say, was millions of dollars in spending in the election that could have gone toward defeating Republicans.
Wahab has since spoken with both Lofgren and Aguilar and they congratulated her on her win, she told KCRA 3 News. But one of Wahab's most vocal supporters, Amar Shergill, a prominent progressive activist in California, told CNN that he still blames party leaders for allowing such a "shocking" intervention against the candidate endorsed by the state party.
"I've never seen anything like it, it was unprecedented," Shergill said. "Lofgren leads the largest congressional delegation in the country. When she makes moves behind the scenes, everybody hears about it. It's impossible for DC leadership not to know what she's doing."
"It was a tough primary but we're looking forward to everyone coalescing around her and putting the primary behind us," said Evan Brown, executive director of the Congressional Progressive Caucus PAC.
Frustrations after bitter primary in Michigan
Meanwhile, in Michigan, progressives are fuming that the House Democrats' campaign arm has refused to publicly promote left-wing Democrat, Will Lawrence, roughly a month after he won a nasty three-way primary there.
At issue: The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has so far declined to add Lawrence to a coveted list of their priority House candidates, in part out of deference to leaders of the Congressional Black Caucus, multiple people involved in discussions about the issue told CNN.
The CBC has yet to endorse Lawrence after their public battle with him during the primary over his 2024 comments criticizing Black political leaders. Lawrence, a White climate activist who recently let his DSA membership lapse, came under fire from senior Black Democrats, including Jeffries and Meeks for saying Black political leaders "defang the White left."
Lawrence, in previous interviews with CNN, has apologized for his "choice of words" in that statement. And some House progressives are "absolutely apoplectic" that party leaders have not yet backed him, according to one of those people.
"We're working on a path forward when it comes to being able to support him," a Black Caucus strategist with knowledge of the situation told CNN.
The list, run by the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, is effectively seen as a "stamp of approval" from party leaders - a flashing sign for party groups and donors to put their support behind the strongest candidates. Lawrence's absence, progressives say, is depriving him of a big fundraising boost to help defeat GOP Rep. Tom Barrett.
The flare-up in Michigan comes after party leaders did get behind a slew of other progressive candidates in key races - including some who defeated party-preferred candidates - such as Randy Villegas in a pivotal California swing seat.
The DCCC and Lawrence's campaign declined to comment. But one person familiar with the inner-workings of the DCCC told CNN that the group has been "working every day" with Lawrence's team to defeat Barrett in November.
Meeks, who runs the Black Caucus's PAC, said he's had "good conversations" with Lawrence over the phone and is looking forward to sitting down with him in Washington soon.
"We'll talk. I think we're going to get that resolved," he said. "If you look at him, compared to who he's running against, we want him to win."

titulo: Trump steps on Vance’s primetime moment and other takeaways from RNC convention’s second night
texto_limpo:
Vice President JD Vance offered Republicans a glimpse of what could be the party's future on Thursday night, as he hammered home a midterm message with overtures to disaffected voters, a pro-family pitch in personal terms, and plenty of red-meat attacks on Democrats.
Then President Donald Trump stepped on stage.
And he stayed there, for more than 25 minutes, riffing about his favorite opera singers, how ugly he thinks Texas Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton is and urging attendees at one point to "cheat like hell" to keep Republicans in control of Congress - all a night after he covered many of the same topics in a rollicking speech of his own.
President Donald Trump closed out the GOP's midterm convention Thursday night by calling on its attendees to vote and pledge to "cheat like hell" to help Republicans keep control of Congress.
It was a jarring end to the GOP's unusual two-day midterm convention in Dallas, which came less than two months before Americans will decide whether the party will retain its House and Senate majorities or hand Democrats power for the last two years of Trump's term.
Faced with an unpopular president, a war with Iran that has sent gas prices rising and historical headwinds, Republicans are seeking to make the midterm elections about the Democrats - casting even the party's more moderate nominees in key races as beholden to its progressive insurgency.
"It's about sending a message to the Democratic Party that if you send your crazies, we're going to send you packing," Vance said of the stakes of November's elections.
But since Trump's ascension a decade ago, Republicans have performed poorly in many elections when his name hasn't been on the ballot. So even as some GOP candidates in competitive races seek to shift voters' focus away from the president, Trump urged the party faithful on Thursday night to pretend he is on the ballot this year.
He led the crowd in an extended pledge to vote, asking them to promise to "go out with my family, my friends ... I don't care if I'm registered or not, I'm going to try and cheat like hell, like they (Democrats) do."
"You know what happens if you don't vote?" Trump said. "You go to hell."
Here are key takeaways from the final night of the GOP's midterm convention:
Vance's 2028 audition
Just as important as what Vance said in his keynote speech closing Thursday night is that he was chosen to fill the most important slot on the schedule aside from Trump's appearances.
The 2028 presidential race will kick into gear immediately after the midterms. Vance hasn't yet said whether he will run, but he is viewed by many Republicans as Trump's heir apparent.
It was on the crowd's mind. At one point during his speech, some Republicans broke into a "48" chant. The president who succeeds Trump will be the nation's 48th.
"We've got to take care of business this November. Then we'll worry about what comes next," a laughing Vance told them.
From the personal references Vance peppered about his wife, Usha, their children, and his grandfather, to the kinds of jokes he delivered, the stylistic differences between the vice president and Trump were obvious.
Like Trump, he waded eagerly into culture wars. But unlike Trump, he focused his message on faith and family values - detailing at length the nation he wants for his newborn son.
"What I want for my family, I want for your family, too," Vance said.
One of the strongest crowd reactions to Vance came in an unscripted moment. A protester interrupted the vice president's speech, and Vance told viewers at home that the protester was holding a Mexican flag.
"If you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there. I'll buy you a plane ticket," Vance said, as the crowd erupted in a "USA" chant.
The convention's big theme: We're more normal than the Democrats
Throughout the two-day convention, most Republican speakers skirted by the Trump administration's most controversial moves, including the war with Iran, a failure to roll back high prices, and tariffs and mass deportation efforts that many voters say have gone too far.
Instead, they highlighted the ascendance of far-left progressives and democratic socialists, and ascribed some of their positions - including policies involving transgender people, calls to defund the police and efforts to disband US Immigration and Customs Enforcement - to the entire Democratic Party.
"Don't give the country over to a bunch of crazy people because you happen to disagree with us on a policy issue here or there," the vice president pleaded with those listening to his remarks. "I'm not asking anybody to agree on every single policy of the administration; what I am asking you to do is to recognize the contrast with the radicals and recognize the achievements of the last 18 months."
The president's eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., highlighted the rise of democratic socialists who have won a handful of House primaries, mostly in deep-blue districts, as well as the Democratic Senate nomination in Florida.
"We should call it what it is: communism," Trump Jr. said.
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. drew on his family lineage as he argued Democrats have abandoned the values of his uncle, President John F. Kennedy, and his father, Robert Kennedy.
"I mourn the fact that neither my father nor my uncle would recognize the Democratic Party of today," he said.
Abdul El-Sayed and Hasan Piker focal points ahead of 9/11 anniversary
The most mentioned Democrat of the night Thursday was Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan Senate nominee.
His prominence is no surprise: Democrats' hopes of netting the four seats they need to take control of the Senate depend in part on El-Sayed retaining the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters. And as Republicans look to cast Democrats as too extreme, they've zeroed in on the progressive firebrand and strident Israel critic as their favorite example.
Repeatedly, Republicans linked El-Sayed to far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who has campaigned with El-Sayed, including appearing with him the day before Michigan's Democratic primary.
Piker is a pro-Palestinian activist and one of the loudest critics of the Israeli government's bombardment in Gaza following Hamas' October 7, attacks. He once said the United States "deserved 9/11" - comments he later acknowledged as "inappropriate," and said he was trying to make a more nuanced point about US foreign policy. El-Sayed has distanced himself from the streamer as his general election campaign has gotten underway.
The day before the 25th anniversary of the <DATE>, attacks, GOP speakers repeatedly invoked those remarks and linked El-Sayed to Piker.
"I never imagined that 25 years after 9/11, I would be running against somebody that campaigns with Hasan Piker, who thinks America deserved it," said El-Sayed's opponent, Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers.
"El-Sayed's biggest booster, a man named Hasan Piker, he said, and I quote: 'America deserved 9/11.' Well, ladies and gentlemen, my mom has a saying: 'You are who you hang with,' and let me tell you, Hasan Piker is who Abdul El-Sayed hangs with," said Michigan Rep. Lisa McClain.
Vance also dedicated several minutes of his remarks to an ongoing feud with El-Sayed.
The vice president had mused in a speech last month that he'd have difficulty going back in time and explaining the current Democratic Party to his late grandfather, who he called "Papaw." Vance in the speech also falsely accused El-Sayed, a practicing Muslim, of wanting to impose Sharia law.
El-Sayed later responded to the speech on X, writing: "So do we think JD is taking Usha with him back in time to meet Papaw, or no?" in reference to Vance's wife, who is Indian American and was raised in a Hindu household.
Vance on Thursday night detailed the back-and-forth and said that "that is what he thinks of my grandfather."
"Abdul looks at him, sees the color of his skin, sees his background, and decides that he could never have loved my wife," Vance said. "Abdul himself was raised by his own white step-grandparents. He knows exactly that kind of bond and what it looks like in a family, and he chose anyway to say that a man like my grandfather couldn't have loved from the bottom of his heart someone who looks like Usha."
El-Sayed previously addressed Vance's response to his critique in an interview with CNN's Kaitlan Collins.
"I believe in an America where any of us - me, his wife, any of us with different-colored skin or who pray different ways - can be just as American as JD and his papaw," El-Sayed said. "But he's not making that argument. He likes to dog-whistle about these things, but when you actually call him out on it, he acts like he would never bring anything like that into our political conversation, despite he and his boss doing that every single day."
Trump's the only one talking about his $5,000 pitch
Trump on Thursday night re-upped the surprise pitch he included in Wednesday night's speech - one that dominated news coverage of the convention: $5,000 for every American adult if Republicans retain their House and Senate majorities in November.
Perhaps more notable is that his vice president didn't once mention the idea.
Nor did other Republican speakers throughout the convention's second night - most of whom had likely prepared their remarks before Trump blindsided many of his administration's own officials with his proposal.
Trump's proposal ignited controversy for a number of reasons: Democrats decried it as a blatant attempt to buy votes. Economists warned it would cause inflation. Trump vacillated in interviews Thursday about whether or not the checks would need the approval of Congress. And no one knew how Trump would pay for the proposal. He said it would come from tariff revenue, but those revenues don't come close to covering the $1 trillion bill for such checks.
"We can do that because our country has never done better. We are taking in trillions of dollars," Trump said Thursday night, dramatically inflating tariff revenues.
A play for independents
Most of the two-day GOP convention was red meat - attacks on Democrats and pitches for Trump's signature achievements, aimed at ginning up the party's base for the sprint to November.
In pictures: The first-ever Republican midterm convention
But New York Rep. Mike Lawler, one of three GOP House members who represents a district former Vice President Kamala Harris won in the 2024 election, had a much different target in mind: Independents and moderate Democrats.
Or, as Lawler put it, voters "who are deeply concerned about the rise of socialism and extremism on the left, but they aren't exactly sold on Republicans either."
He used his own public and private disagreements with Trump to make his case. He acknowledged that Trump had called him a "pain in the ass" and even did a convincing impersonation of Trump mocking him.
Lawler advocated for lifting the cap on the amount of state and local taxes residents could deduct on their federal income tax returns - an issue that matters to high-income states like New York. He threatened to oppose Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act if the measure was not included.
"The truth is that the president and I don't always agree, and that's OK. After all, we're both New Yorkers. We argue. We tell each other what we think," Lawler said. "There's even some profanity."
"What I learned about President Trump behind closed doors is that if you're willing to make your case and fight for what you believe in, he's willing to listen," he said.
The speech stood out as a rare example of a Republican candidate even acknowledging any daylight between themselves and Trump at the convention. For the most part, speakers either lavished praise on the president or avoided mentioning him and attacked their own Democratic opponents in this year's elections.
Speakers remember Charlie Kirk, one year after his assassination
Thursday marked one year since a gunman shot and killed conservative activist Charlie Kirk during a Turning Point USA event on a college campus in Utah.
Trump paid tribute to Kirk's widow, Erika Kirk, on Wednesday night. And several speakers acknowledged Kirk on Thursday.
"History will record that your father was a great man," Vance said in a message aimed at Kirk's children. He called Kirk a friend, and recalled him cheering Vance on when he last spoke at a Republican convention, after accepting the vice presidential nomination in 2024.
Trump Jr. said Kirk was a good friend, and said he "had already inspired hundreds of thousands of young people to take up the cause of liberty and to fight for it."
Other speakers, including Kennedy and former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, also remembered Kirk.
Leaders of the organization he co-founded vowed to continue with his mission.
"One year later there is something wonderfully defiant about the fact that his voice has not grown quieter - it has multiplied," Lucas Miles, the vice president of Turning Point USA, said at the convention.

titulo: Ed Sheeran tour: Macklemore dropped, other openers quit
texto_limpo:
Ed Sheeran's international tour has been thrown into crisis, with one opening act, the rapper Macklemore, dropped from the tour's US dates for his onstage support of Palestine, and all of the British singer's other openers quitting to protest the removal.
On Monday, Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots, said he would bar Macklemore from performing at Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts this month. Macklemore, who made pro-Palestinian remarks during shows in New Jersey, said he had been removed from the rest of Sheeran's American tour as well.
"Based on Macklemore's recent actions, material shared from the stage during Ed Sheeran's shows in New Jersey, and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community, we determined that his participation in the September 25th and 26th concerts at Gillette Stadium would cross that line," Kraft said in a statement.
In 2014, Macklemore publicly apologized for performing while wearing a hooked false nose, wig and fake beard, which he called a "random costume" but which observers widely read as an antisemitic caricature. Kraft did not respond to a question about whether he was referring to that incident or to something else when he accused Macklemore of past antisemitism.
On Tuesday, Finneas, a producer who is also Billie Eilish's brother, the Irish singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe, the Irish band Beoga and the Danish band Lukas Graham all withdrew from their opening slots on the tour, expressing support for both Macklemore and the Palestinian people.
Macklemore, a rapper best known for 2012's "Thrift Shop," has publicly advocated for Palestinian rights since Israel began its years-long bombing campaign in Gaza after the October 7 attacks. Opening for Sheeran earlier this month at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, the rapper wore a black-and-white keffiyeh tied around his neck.
"A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place, was so I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: Free Palestine," he said, according to video of the event. He added that "to all of my Jewish brothers and sisters, criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you."
Macklemore has regularly performed at pro-Palestinian rallies since 2023. In 2024, he released "Hind's Hall," named after the building taken over by Columbia student protesters, who renamed it in honor of Hind Rajab, a 5-year-old Palestinian girl killed by Israeli soldiers in Gaza.
His comments at Sheeran's show prompted criticism from the singer Pink and a petition against his appearances. On Monday, Macklemore announced on Instagram he'd been dropped from Sheeran's remaining US tour dates.
Macklemore has pointed the blame squarely at Kraft, who owns Gillette Stadium, where Sheeran and Macklemore were scheduled to perform later this month. Kraft, Macklemore said, had "rallied some of the other stadium owners" and given Sheeran an ultimatum: "if Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play in our venues."
Kraft, an advocate for Israel who withdrew funding for Columbia University to rebuke the school for its handling of protests against the war in Gaza, confirmed that he chose to cancel Macklemore's performances at Gillette Stadium. He didn't address Macklemore's claims that he had "rallied" other stadium owners, and did not respond to requests for more information.
"This decision is not about diminishing the suffering of innocent Palestinians or denying anyone the right to advocate on their behalf," Kraft said in his statement. "Too many lives have been lost and there has been too much suffering, but only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas is not honest and only advances more divisiveness and hate."
Sheeran placed the blame on the concert promoter, who he said forced his hand. "After Macklemore's performances at my New Jersey shows, venues on my upcoming tour dates communicated that they would pull the shows if he was still supporting," he said on Instagram Tuesday. "Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine." The promoter didn't respond to a request for comment.
Chilling effect
Legally, under the First Amendment, Kraft and other people who privately own stadiums have the right to choose who performs at their venues, said Lee Rowland, the executive director of the National Coalition Against Censorship. But "that doesn't mean that that's healthy for our democracy or good for free expression," Rowland said.
Rowland said the cancellation of Macklemore's tour dates "illustrates the immense power that money has over our public discourse."
Macklemore was scheduled to open for Sheeran at seven more stadiums in the US. Several of those are publicly owned. The remaining venues did not respond to requests for comment.
Among them is AT&T Stadium, which is owned by the city of Arlington, Texas. AT&T Stadium is scheduled to host a sold-out show later this year by Ye, who made a spate of antisemitic comments that he now attributes to a brain injury and untreated bipolar disorder, and who is selling out shows in the US.
The Macklemore cancellation will likely have a chilling effect on other artists, Rowland said.
"We are undoubtedly going to see widespread self-censorship, so that artists ensure their content is uncontroversial and anodyne enough not to offend a promoter or a stadium owner that would then deprive the audience of their performance."
In his statement, Sheeran, one of the world's best-selling and most-streamed artists, said he was "not complicit" and defended his silence around "the conflict between Israel and Palestine."
"I have my personal views on this devastating conflict," he said. "Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care."
The children's entertainer and advocate Ms. Rachel, who has been a leading humanitarian critic of the war in Gaza, called Sheeran out for his public neutrality, writing on Instagram, "Ed Sheeran is making a political statement to his fans when he does a concert to support Ukraine, but considers Palestine too dangerous and political."
Beyond his fellow tour members quitting in protest, Macklemore received nods of support from Reps. Ilhan Omar and Pramila Jayapal and the musicians Zara Larsson and PinkPantheress.
In his statement, Macklemore sought to refocus attention on Gaza, where more than 70,000 people - many of them women and children - have been killed.
Sheeran "told me that the words 'Free Palestine' and the image of the Palestinian flag were hurtful to a lot of people he spoke with," Macklemore said.
"I told him that if those words were more offensive than tens of thousands of Palestinian children being killed by Israel, then there was a fundamental disconnect between where those people stood and where I stood."

titulo: Son of Israeli ambassador to US critically injured in West Bank ramming attack | CNN
texto_limpo:
The son of Israeli Ambassador to the US Yechiel Leiter was critically injured in a ramming attack in the occupied West Bank on Wednesday afternoon, according to regional authorities, one day before Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's scheduled speech at the United Nations.
Neria Leiter, a reserve soldier manning a checkpoint near the settlement of Beit Horon, was rushed to a hospital in Jerusalem, according to emergency response services.
"Neria needs a miracle," Leiter said in a statement on social media. "I believe in the power of prayer, and I believe that when the people of Israel unite, miracles happen."
The driver of the car, 29-year-old Mahmoud Muhammad Mahmoud Suleiman, a Palestinian from the nearby village of Beit Ur al-Tahta, was shot and killed at the scene of the attack, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health.
Hamas praised the attack in a statement Wednesday, describing it as a "natural response" to Israeli actions in the West Bank and Jerusalem. The militant group in the Gaza Strip called for increased resistance against Israel but did not claim responsibility for the attack.
Leiter's elder son, 39-year-old Moshe Yedidya Leiter, was killed fighting in Gaza in <DATE> in the first weeks of the war triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel the month before.
The ramming attack occurred just days after a shooting in the West Bank on the eve of the Jewish high holiday of Yom Kippur. On Sunday morning, Netanel Shukrun, a father of six from the settlement of Alei Zahav, was shot and killed while bathing at a natural spring in the West Bank as part of the holiday customs. Shukrun's 16-year-old son credited his father with saving his life when he shouted out a warning to take cover.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) arrested the suspected shooter at a hospital near the West Bank city of Ramallah, the military said Sunday. Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called for the death penalty in the case under a new law applying capital punishment to terrorism and nationalistic murders.
After the shooting, Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, the IDF chief of staff, said: "The IDF is on high alert, deployed and prepared with soldiers reinforced across all sectors, including throughout the fast. Our mission is clear and ongoing - to thwart terrorism, act decisively against every threat, and protect the citizens of the State of Israel."
Since October 7, Israel has carried out waves of widescale military operations in the West Bank intended to target what officials view as centers of terrorist activity. The operations have led to the displacement of tens of thousands of Palestinians across the territory and military raids into Palestinian villages.
"Terrorism currently in Judea and Samaria is at its lowest level in decades," Defense Minister Israel Katz said in early September, using the biblical name for the West Bank, "and we will take all necessary steps to prevent terrorism from rearing its head again."
This is a developing story and will be updated.
